d_sv_content.name: Clinical Testing of Canine T Cells Engineered to Target Soft Tissue Sarcoma with Oral Immunotherapy
d_sv_content.tagline: Help us test a new combination therapy for soft tissue sarcoma in dogs.
d_sv_content.description:
This study is evaluating a new type of cancer treatment for dogs with soft tissue sarcoma. The treatment uses your dog’s own immune cells (called T cells) to help fight cancer.

A blood sample is collected (about 3-4 tablespoons), and the T cells are modified in a lab to better recognize and attack cancer cells. These upgraded cells (called CAR T cells) are then given back to your dog through an IV infusion.

Dogs in this study may also receive oral immunotherapy medications to help improve how well the treatment works.

The goal of this study is to determine if this treatment is safe and effective in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma.

d_sv_content.name: Feasibility and dose-optimization clinical trial of local immunotherapy for solid tumors in canine cancer patients
d_sv_content.tagline: Intra-tumoral T-cell Engager Therapy for Canine Soft Tissue Sarcoma
d_sv_content.description:
WHY IS THIS STUDY BEING DONE?

Immunotherapies are a class of anti-cancer treatments that work by activating a patient’s own immune system to fight specific diseases, including cancer. A number of immunotherapies have been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in humans in a wide range of diseases, including cancer. While these therapies have shown positive results in cancers of blood cells, they have had more limited successes in solid tumors like soft tissue sarcoma. This is thought to be in part because it is hard to get enough of the drug into the tumor when it is given through the blood stream (intravenously) without causing serious side effects. To overcome this limitation, this research study will use injections of immunotherapies directly through the skin into the tumor (intra-tumoral injections). 


The primary goal of this research study is to test whether it is safe and feasible to treat tumors by injecting them with a certain type of immunotherapy called T-cell engagers (TCEs).  A T cell is a special kind of white blood cell that attacks sick cells in your body, including virus-infected cells and cancer cells. TCEs are a new kind of cancer immunotherapy that helps a patient’s own T cells find and kill cancer cells. They work like a connector: one end sticks to a cancer cell, and the other end sticks to a T cell. By pulling the two cells together, the TCE helps the T cell recognize the cancer cell and activate its killing response. In this research study, two different TCEs will be tested together (TCE combination). They work in much the same way, but each one attaches to different markers on cancer cells and T cells. Because they target different markers, the two treatments can help T cells kill cancer cells more effectively, even at lower doses of each TCE, which helps reduce the chance of harmful side effects. The goal is to make the therapy work better while still keeping patients safe.


The study will test different doses of TCEs per injection, different numbers of injections placed into the tumor itself, and the product used to dilute the TCEs. The TCE combination will be diluted either in sterile saline (a solution of salt and water) or in hydrogel (a water-based gel). The hydrogel’s job is to slowly release the drugs into the tumor, with the goal to keep the cancer cells exposed to the drugs for a longer time. This may help the treatment work better and could also reduce side effects. The TCE combination will also be mixed with sterile fluorescent dye(s) that will help researchers track where the injections were placed in the tumor. The fluorescent dye(s) have already been used in multiple canine and human clinical trials with no known side effects.  


The “investigational” part of the study are the intratumoral injections of the TCE combinations diluted in sterile saline or hydrogel. These TCEs are investigational drugs, which means they have not yet been approved by the FDA or the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) for use in dogs or other species. The purpose of this study is to test the safety and the biological effect of the TCE combination in canine patients with soft tissue sarcoma (STS), rather than to specifically provide medical treatment to the enrolled patient.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: It is not currently known whether dogs enrolled in this study will benefit from intra-tumoral treatment with these TCEs at these doses or at any dose. This is one of the questions the study sponsor is interested in answering through this study. A benefit may come as an anti-tumor response, a reduced risk of tumor recurrence or spread after removal, and/or an improvement in quality of life and survival should the treatment result in an anti-tumor response or lowered risk of spread or recurrence. It is possible that the study drug will have no clinical benefit. It is also possible that a patient enrolled in this study may experience negative side effects from the drug.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks:
WHAT ARE THE RISKS OF THE STUDY?


Risks to patient: 


The standard laboratory tests (blood work), ultrasound, sedation, anesthesia, and surgery carry the same risks they would if the patient were undergoing these procedures outside of the study. The TCEs under investigation have the potential to cause unwanted side effects. These unwanted side effects, anticipated to the best of our current knowledge based on studies in dogs with various tumor types, are also described below.


Blood sample collection: A small needle will be inserted into the vein of the enrolled patient to take blood samples. The total amount of blood to be obtained for study related procedures at any given visit is typically less that 5ml (roughly 1 teaspoon). Risks associated with blood draw may include some discomfort, mild irritation at the collection site, bruising, and rarely infection. Blood draws are part of standard of care for anesthesia and cancer treatment in general and may be done whether the patient participates in this study or not. The addition of intratumorally injected TCEs is not expected to alter the safety of blood sample collection. 


Tumor ultrasound: There are no known risks associated with performing ultrasound other than possible mild discomfort from pressure placed on the ultrasound probe throughout the examination. 


Surgery: The surgical protocol will be performed according to standard of care, which means that there is nothing experimental about the surgery portion of the study. There is currently no evidence to indicate that any of these standard surgical and anesthesia risks will be increased by the study drug evaluated in this study. The surgeon can discuss any standard surgery risks, including bleeding after surgery, infection at the surgery site, poor wound healing, and death.


Sedation/Anesthesia: Risks of sedation and anesthesia include low blood pressure, abnormal heart rhythms, bad reactions to the anesthesia drugs, and rarely, respiratory and/or cardiac arrest and death.


Immunotherapy Injections: The immunotherapy injections will occur through small needles, similar to those used for standard vaccines. Predictable risks associated with these TCE injections include temporary pain, minor bleeding from the injection sites, redness, and irritation at the injection site, particularly if the immune system responds to the injected agents. These TCEs are expected to affect the immune system. Therefore, temporary changes in the numbers of different immune cells within the tumor are anticipated. However, these changes are not expected to require treatment. At the veterinarian’s discretion, pain medication may be given before the tumor injections to reduce any discomfort. This is optional because the injections may not be any more painful than routine shots, blood draws, or other procedures that usually don’t require pain relief.


Human patients in clinical trials of other TCEs - given at higher doses into the bloodstream rather than directly into tumors - have sometimes experienced flu‑like symptoms, low blood pressure, and other side effects. In a prior canine clinical study testing intratumoral injection of a different TCE (not being used in this study), one patient experienced liver enzyme elevations and a systemic inflammatory response that resolved within a few days. Clinical signs included abdominal pain, two episodes of vomiting, dull mentation, increased heart rate, low blood pressure, and pale mucous membranes. Although this study seeks to reduce these risks through careful selection of the TCEs and the intratumoral doses to be used, these and other side effects, such as irritation at the injection site, release of release of chemicals in the body that can cause an overactive immune response, or injury to the intestines, hormonal system, heart, brain, lungs, and/or skin could occur. To reduce the risks of side effects in treated patients, all patients will be given oral diphenhydramine (Benadryl) 1-2 hours before injection (to help lower the risk of whole‑body allergic or anaphylactic reactions), patients will be monitored closely overnight following administration of the TCE, and the dose will be adjusted carefully between dose cohorts.


The dose and treatment schedule utilized in this study were selected to minimize risk experienced by each patient enrolled on this study. There also may be other side effects or risks that we cannot predict. Many side effects go away shortly after the drug treatment, but in some cases side effects can be serious or long-lasting or permanent.


During the course of this study, we may find out more information about the study drug, its safety, or efficacy that could be important. This information, once learned, will be made available.
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

  1. Informed owner consent for trial participation.
  2. At least one measurable superficial presumed soft tissue sarcoma (STS) lesion (primary or recurrent tumor) that is accessible for percutaneous injection and for which there is a planned surgical intervention. 
  3. Tumor mass must be at least three times the volume to be injected (i.e. 900 mm3 in volume if 3x100 ml of TCE in saline or hydrogel will be injected) and must have a depth of at least 1.7 cm to accommodate needle length (1.25 cm) and minimum surgical pathology margin (0.4 cm).
  4. No medical contraindication to sedation, general anesthesia, or surgery.
  5. Life expectancy > 8 weeks.

Favorable performance status based on modified Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) criteria Grade 0 or 1
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
Exclusion Criteria:

  1. Weight less than 5 kg.
  2. Tumors that are anticipated by the Investigator to lack a sufficient volume of viable tumor tissue for injection due to tumor size, location, or other features based on any available pre-operative imaging (CT or ultrasound) or pathology reports describing extensive necrosis, cystic areas, or other non-viable tumor tissue.
  3. Tumors near or involving critical structures for which, in the opinion of the treating clinician, injection would pose undue risk to the patient. 
  4. Significant co-morbidities that could, in the opinion of the Investigator, interfere with adherence to the study’s procedures or requirements, or otherwise compromise the study’s objectives.
  5. History of immune-mediated disease (immune-mediated polyarthritis [IMPA], immune-mediated hemolytic anemia [IMHA], immune-mediated thrombocytopenia [ITP], myasthenia gravis, etc.) 
  6. Creatinine > 1.5x upper limit of normal (ULN)
  7. Bilirubin > 2x ULN 
  8. Hematocrit or packed cell volume < 25%
  9. Platelets < 100,000 cells/ul
  10. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) > 2.5x ULN
  11. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) ≥ 5x ULN
  12. Use of anti-coagulants ≤ 2 weeks prior to injection.
  13. Use of any nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) ≤ 3 days prior to injection.
  14. Use of JAK inhibitors (e.g., Apoquel, Zenrelia, Numelvi) ≤ 14 days prior to injection.
  15. Use of cyclosporine ≤ 30 days prior to injection.
  16. Use of corticosteroids ≤ 7 days prior to injection.
  17. Use of immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g. Gilvetmab) ≤ 3 months prior to injection
  18. Use of other T-cell targeting agents (CAR-T Cells, monoclonal antibodies (OX40, 4-1BB, etc.) ≤ 3 months prior to injection.
d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name: Multiple different T-cell engagers (TCE) will be delivered by injection intra-tumor with either sterile saline or hydrogel. The TCEs are engineered antibodies that bind to two targets, one on a tumor cell (B7-H3 or PD-L1) and one on a T-cell (CD3 or CD28).
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_name: Determine the safety and feasibility of intratumoral delivery of TCEs in canine patients.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_measure: Occurrence and severity of adverse events according to Veterinary Cooperative Oncology Group-Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (VCOG-CTCAE v2).
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_endpoint: The safety of a dose will be determined by the number of patients, if any, who experience a dose-limiting toxicity. Dose limiting toxicities for this study will be defined as adverse events greater than or equal to grade 3 (as defined by VCOG-CTCAE v2) that do not improve to grade 2 or less with outpatient therapy within 3 days.
d_avma_studycontent_data.sec_outcome1_name: Optimize the TCE concentration and number of injection sites ahead of a Phase II study.
d_avma_studycontent_data.sec_outcome1_measure: Histopathology and Immunohistochemistry
d_avma_studycontent_data.sec_outcome1_endpoint: Evidence of immune activation and immune-mediated cancer cell death via necrotic zone on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained slides and abundance of T-cells proximal to injection tract (e.g., within 3.14 mm2). Immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining and H&E images to assess biological response of the treatments.

d_sv_content.name: Autologous Cancer Vaccine with Checkpoint Inhibitor for Treatment of Canine Osteosarcoma
d_sv_content.tagline: Autologous Cancer Vaccine with Checkpoint Inhibitor for Treatment of Canine Osteosarcoma
d_sv_content.description:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the safety and efficacy of K9-ACV, an autologous killed tumor cell vaccine combined with a novel checkpoint inhibitor (CD200AR-L), compared to standard-of-care chemotherapy for the treatment of canine appendicular osteosarcoma (OSA). K9-ACV has safely been used in over 1,000 dogs and the vaccine has been shown to display safety in a previous study (without the addition of the checkpoint inhibitor). By evaluating K9-ACV, this trial aims to advance safer, immune-based treatment options for canine cancer that may offer comparable or superior outcomes to chemotherapy.


Participating patients will be required to complete standard pre-enrollment screening that involves a physical exam, blood work, chest x-rays, and abdominal ultrasound. If the patient passes the screening, they will undergo limb amputation and be randomly assigned to the K9-ACV group or the carboplatin group. Patients in the K9-ACV group will receive an intradermal injection of the checkpoint inhibitor and then will return to the study site 24 hours later for the vaccine administration. Vaccines will be given every 3 weeks for a total of 3 treatments. Patients will return at 4, 6, and 8 months after initial vaccine administration for a physical exam, blood work, and x-rays. Patients in the chemotherapy group will be treated every 3 weeks for a total of 4 treatments. Patients will return at 4, 6, and 8 months after initial chemotherapy treatment for a physical exam, blood work, and x-rays.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: Increased survival time and/or quality of life after administration of K9-ACV.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks:
Immunotherapy – local redness, swelling, or pain around the injection site; mild fever, lethargy; nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, reduced appetite; rare risk of severe allergic reaction that would require anti-inflammatory therapy.


Chemotherapy – bone marrow suppression (low white cell or platelet counts); gastrointestinal upset (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea); fever, lethargy. If untreated for bone marrow suppression, rarely dogs could become septic and require intensive antibiotic therapy.
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
- Dog is ≥ 1 year of age and greater or equal to 20 kilograms in weight.

- Dog is in good general health, with the exception of appendicular osteosarcoma, Stage IIB.

- Dog had cytologic and/or histologic confirmation of appendicular osteosarcoma, Stage IIB.

- Dog had a vaccine produced from its tumor according to the Outline of Production.
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
- Dog received concurrent or previous therapy (within 30 days) with immune-modulating drugs (e.g., cyclosporine, Apoquel, Cytopoint, prednisone, any chemotherapy, etc.)

- Dog received NSAIDs less than three days before immunization with the IVP.

- Dogs have received prior chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or bisphosphonates for their appendicular osteosarcoma.

- Dog has any uncontrolled medical condition that is likely to be disruptive to the intent of the study.

- Dog is known to be pregnant or likely to become pregnant during the study.

- Dog is lactating or intended for breeding during the study.

- Dog is participating in another therapeutic study.

- Dog is not available for the duration of the study.
d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name: The vaccine for this trial is an autologous (derived from the individual's own body) killed tumor cell vaccine combined with a canine-optimized CpG ODN adjuvant. This vaccine and adjuvant combination has demonstrated safety and preliminary efficacy in a 2016 publication where 85% of dogs developed an augmented IgG response to autologous tumor antigens and several dogs lived beyond expected survival time. In this study, a secondary adjuvant, CD200 activation receptor ligand (CD200AR-L), will be administered intradermally alongside the vaccine. A similar vaccine design in dogs with spontaneous brain tumors (glioma) demonstrated significant improvement in survival compared to tumor vaccine alone.

d_sv_content.name: Enhanced Ethanol Ablation for Feline Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
d_sv_content.description: Some cancer patients have a poor prognosis, despite intensive multimodal therapy (e.g., surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy). In other cases, these treatments are likely to improve outcome but are inaccessible (e.g., financial, scheduling and/or geographical limitations). Thus, there is an immense need for treatments that offer effective tumor control and palliation, and that ideally can be given at low-cost in the primary care setting. We have recently demonstrated proof-of-concept for a low-cost effective option, called enhanced ethanol ablation. Ethanol ablation (intratumoral injectionof pure ethanol) was originally used for human liver cancer, achieving survival rates similar to surgical resection for small tumors. However, conventional ethanol ablation is ineffective for superficial, large, and/or poorly encapsulated lesions, and requires large injection volumes. Enhanced ethanol ablation involves controlled injection of an ethyl cellulose- ethanol mixture directly into the tumor. When mixed with ethyl cellulose, a water-insoluble ethanol-based gel is formed. We have shown this caused complete regression in 7 of 7 chemically-induced tumors in the hamster oral cavity while dramatically reducing the required injection volume. Now, we will perform a pilot study to evaluate safety and efficacy in feline oral squamous cell carcinomas, which serves as a model for other large, superficial and invasive tumors. Cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma (mandibular and maxillary) will be enrolled. They will have basic staging tests performed, and then undergo anesthesia for a intratumoral injection of ethyl cellulose-ethanol. The tumor will be imaged using CT, before and after injection. Cats will be hospitalized overnight for observation, after this first injection. They will then return for periodic recheck exams to evaluate for toxicity and changes in tumor size. Depending on response to the first injection, cats may be eligible for up to 2 booster injections. Cats will be dismissed from the study at the time of local disease progression, or after 6 months of follow-up.

d_sv_content.name: Ethos Precision Medicine Umbrella Study for Hemangiosarcoma (Ethos-PUSH)
d_sv_content.tagline: Ethos-PUSH: Hemangiosarcoma
d_sv_content.description: Canine splenic hemangiosarcoma is an aggressive cancer with limited treatment options available. Dogs presenting with this disease often have spontaneous internal bleeding that results in sudden onset of weakness or collapse. Although this is a common consequence for hemangiosarcoma, any other tumor of the spleen can spontaneously bleed resulting in these same changes. Dogs who have a bleeding splenic tumor must undergo surgery to remove the spleen (called splenectomy). This procedure both removes the source of life-threatening hemorrhage and provides tissue samples for making a final diagnosis. Roughly 40% of dogs have benign splenic disease causing the internal bleeding and will be cured with surgery alone. Many of the remaining dogs will have hemangiosarcoma as the cause of their bleeding and will require chemotherapy following surgery to delay or prevent metastatic disease. For dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma, the combination of surgery and chemotherapy has been estimated to provide median survival times of 4-9 months with only a small percentage of dogs surviving to 2 years. Ethos-PUSH embarks on a journey to improve the outcome of canine hemangiosarcoma by furthering our understanding of this disease. Dogs confirmed to have hemangiosarcoma will be randomized to receive 1 of 4 treatments. These treatment groups include standard therapies and novel therapies that have been selected as potential targets against previously defined genomic alterations in hemangiosarcoma. Treatment arms will be compared to determine a best protocol, which will serve as the benchmark for future treatment studies. Furthermore, tumor and blood samples will be collected and serve as platforms for nationwide collaborations to improve the molecular understanding of this disease and match molecular biomarkers with treatment response to specific therapeutics. This comprehensive approach is designed to bring about curative outcomes for dogs suffering from this aggressive cancer. A 501(c)(3) nonprofit incubator of scientific innovation, Ethos Discovery has developed the most innovative scientific portfolio in the field of animal health and delivers answers to our clinical research questions through rigorous clinical trials made available to pet patients. The mission of Ethos Discovery is to improve health outcomes for humans and animals with complex medical problems. We are agnostic to the source of good ideas and uniquely positioned, with the support of Ethos Veterinary Health, to reach patients and doctors nationally and partner with key leaders in their field internationally. This flexibility provides us the opportunity to pursue impactful research that will make a difference where it is most important, at the point of care and for the benefit of patients and families in the community.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: All dogs with hemoperitoneum that are enrolled into this study will receive a $1,000 credit towards the cost of their surgery. Dogs that receive a diagnosis of hemangiosarcoma are eligible to enter a fully funded follow up study (no cost to the pet owner), giving them access to treatments that were selected based on genomic analysis of hemangiosarcoma and wouldn't otherwise be available.

Even though risks are considered low, each dog may respond differently and side effects are possible.Possibleside effects can include gastrointestinal upset, bone marrow suppression, toxicity tothe heart, allergic reactions, local reactions at the site of injection, and death.

d_sv_content.name: Minimally Invasive Metastasectomy in Canines (MIMIC) Trial
d_sv_content.tagline: Video Assisted Lung Tumor Removal
d_sv_content.description: Following surgical removal of the primary tumor and treatment with chemotherapy, the spread of cancer to the lungs (metastasis) is the most common cause of mortality in dogs with many tumors. A distinctive feature of lung metastases in human patients is the surprising benefit that can result from surgical removal of the lung metastases. The use of surgery to manage lung metastases in dogs has been described but is not commonly used due to the presumed post-surgical complications associated with conventional open chest surgery (thoracotomy). Innovations in minimally invasive surgery have created a new opportunity to include surgical removal of lung metastases with a reduced potential of complications when compared to the conventional thoracotomy techniques. Conventional thoracotomy techniques can be replaced by thoracoscopy, a surgical technique using miniature incisions in the chest to allow for removal of lung metastases with the assistance of a magnified video camera. This approach has the potential to significantly minimize the pain, potential complications, and recovery time in patients compared to what is observed with conventional thoracotomy techniques. Using minimally invasive surgery, specifically video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS), we predict patients will be recovered from the procedure within 2 days and will be able to begin to return to normal life. The goal of our study is to assess the feasibility and tolerability of VATS for lung metastasis and eventually deliver this care as an outpatient procedure. A 501(c)(3) nonprofit incubator of scientific innovation, Ethos Discovery has developed the most innovative scientific portfolio in the field of animal health and delivers answers to our clinical research questions through rigorous clinical trials made available to pet patients. The mission of Ethos Discovery is to improve health outcomes for humans and animals with complex medical problems. We are agnostic to the source of good ideas and uniquely positioned, with the support of Ethos Veterinary Health, to reach patients and doctors nationally and partner with key leaders in their field internationally. This flexibility provides us the opportunity to pursue impactful research that will make a difference where it is most important, at the point of care and for the benefit of patients and families in the community.

d_sv_content.name: COTC033: Repurposing Vaccine Immunity to Treat Cancers: Validation in Canine Patients
d_sv_content.tagline: Using Immunity from Vaccines to Treat Cancer
d_sv_content.description: This clinical trial led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) assesses the safety and effectiveness of a Vaccine Peptide Library (VPL) when given to dogs with cancer. This clinical trial conducted in pet dogs with cancer is designed to test whether the immune responses generated through routine vaccination against common viruses can be re-directed toward cancer cells. The approach appears to work in mouse models of cancer, and we are interested in evaluating it in pet dogs that have naturally occurring cancers that are very similar to humans. If successful, this research would help develop safe, effective, and low-cost ways of treating cancer that would benefit a wide variety of patients, especially those that live in communities with minimal access to cutting-edge cancer care (such as developing and low-resource countries). Studies in dogs with cancer will complement currently open human trials designed to test new doses and effects of this agent. As part of this study, your dog will be randomized to receive one of two vaccine protocols: either combination treatment with Shingrix/Garadasil vaccines or a rabies vaccine. Your dog will come to the Veterinary Teaching Hospital for the primer phase, which includes 1-3 weekly injections of the vaccines. Two weeks later, they will return to start weekly visits for injection of the VPL directly into the tumor for 8 weeks. Dogs will be treated with diphenhydramine (Benadryl) prior to the injection and then will be monitored for 4-6 hours post-injection. One final visit will be required one week after the last injection (total length of study 12-14 weeks). Physical exam and blood collections for study purposes will be performed at each visit. A complete blood count will be performed every week during the treatment phase; blood and urine for serum chemistry profile and urinalysis will also be collected on Weeks 1, 5, and 9. Chest x-rays +/- abdominal ultrasound will be checked prior to the primer vaccine and at Week 9. Lymph node aspirates for study purposes will be obtained at Weeks 1, 5, and 9 of the treatment phase. Biopsies of your dogs tumor will also be collected prior to the first dose of the drug (pre-treatment), on Week 5, Week 5 at 24hrs, and Week 9 depending on how your dog has responded to therapy. Each of these biopsy sessions will occur under anesthesia, either local (sedation with anesthetic) or general.

d_sv_content.name: Efficacy and safety of a novel anti-cancer therapeutic for the treatment of metastatic mammary carcinoma in cats
d_sv_content.tagline: feline metastatic mammary carcinoma
d_sv_content.description: Purpose of Study:Mammary tumors are a commonly encountered cancer in cats, particularly in females, with 80-90% of masses diagnosed as malignant (carcinoma). Mammary carcinoma in cats parallels breast cancer in humans with regards to receptor expression profile and propensity of metastasis. The median survival time in cats ranges from 6 months to several years, depending on tumor size and grade. Greater than 60% of cats have more than one tumor at diagnosis, with the majority being high grade. The objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and efficacy of a novel therapeutic targeting miR-10b, a molecule responsible for viability of metastatic cells in cats with mammary carcinoma. This multipurpose therapy has a previously demonstrated efficacy in halting breast cancer invasion and metastasis in mice. The advantage of our novel therapeutic over existing drugs is that it can also be used to visualize primary and metastatic lesions in vivo by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Studies in cats with mammary carcinoma will help bring this therapeutic into clinic to treat human breast cancer.

d_sv_content.name: Observational Study of a Novel Canine Cancer Diet
d_sv_content.tagline: Observational Study of a Novel Canine Cancer Diet
d_sv_content.description:
When patients undergo fractionated radiation therapy, maintaining appetite, consistent stools, and body weight are incredibly important for patient well-being and quality of life. The most common non-radiation complications in dogs undergoing these longer radiation protocols include diarrhea, vomiting or regurgitation, and decreased appetite. When these complications happen in patients, both owners and clinicians attempt to offer a multitude of foods, home cooked diets, probiotics, appetite stimulants, anti-nausea medications, or antibiotics. Recently nutritionists and veterinarians at a well-known pet food manufacturer developed a prescription diet designed to specifically help nourish and support dogs that are fighting cancer. This diet is highly digestible and contains a proprietary blend of prebiotic fibers to help support a healthy gastrointestinal microbiome to provide consistent stool quality. The goal of this study is to evaluate the acceptance of the novel diet through food intake and eating enthusiasm data by dogs undergoing daily, definitive intent radiation therapy, and to examine the differences in body weight changes, muscle condition scoring, body condition scoring, body fat index, quality of life, and stool consistency over time in dogs receiving the novel vs control diet.


If your dog participates in this study, he/she will have blood work, urine panel, fecal analysis, and will be randomized to receive one of the two study foods during radiation therapy. Blood work and fecal analysis will be performed prior to starting radiation therapy, half way through radiation, at the end of the radiation protocol and two weeks after completing radiation. Urine panel will be performed prior to starting radiation, at the final radiation dose, and at the two week recheck. We will assess intake of the diet and enthusiasm of the diet twice weekly. We ask that you also record food intake and eating enthusiasm twice a week, fecal scores at each defecation, and quality of life weekly with provided guides and questionnaires. You and your clinical team will be blinded to which diet your dog is receiving, but this will be revealed at the conclusion of the study period.

d_sv_content.name: Cell Therapy for Metastatic Osteosarcoma
d_sv_content.tagline: CAR iNKT cell therapy for metastatic osteosarcoma
d_sv_content.description: In this study we will investigate the therapeutic potential of a type of white blood cell known as invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells that are made from the blood of a healthy donor dog. iNKT cells are potent immune cells that kill cancer cells in mouse models and in some human cancer patients. In this study, we will use iNKT cells that express a cancer targeting receptor known as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR). The CAR directs the modified iNKT cells to the cancer cells which are then killed. The CAR-iNKT cells also will further activate the patient's own immune system to help kill the cancer cells. The purpose of this study is to determine the safety of CAR-iNKT cells, their maximum tolerated dose, how long they will remain in the patient and their effectiveness against bone cancer that has spread to the lungs.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: The overall goal is to see either stable disease or regression of established pulmonary metastatic osteosarcoma lesions.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks: Possible side effects include cytokine release syndrome (high fever, lethargy, inappetence, low blood pressure, fast heart rate, nausea, vomiting), Graft versus Host Disease (GVHD) (CAR-iNKT cells could attack patient's own tissues causing skin ulcerations, gastrointestinal symptoms, vomiting, and/or diarrhea), in target, off tumor cytotoxicity (damage to tissues in the body other than the cancer cells), dyspnea and tachypnea (difficulty breathing, rapid breathing), bone marrow suppression (increased susceptibility to infection), lethargy, fever, anorexia, nausea and vomiting, allergic reactions during cell infusion (facial and tongue edema, pruritis, vomiting, diarrhea).
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria: Dogs with a histopathological diagnosis of B7-H3+ appendicular osteosarcoma (the expression of the target protein B7H3, will be determined by the study team, who will perform immunohistochemistry on a portion of the archived tumor taken from the initial site in the leg either pre-amputation or at the time of amputation), dogs who have undergone standard of care amputation followed by 4 to 6 doses of carboplatin, dogs who have not received cytotoxic chemotherapy for at least 8 weeks, dogs with evidence of pulmonary metastatic disease, adequate hematologic parameters, and hepatic and renal function, no significant co-morbidities, expected survival time of at least 2 months at the time of enrollment, body weight of at least 18kg.
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria: Dogs without evidence of B7-H3 expression on primary appendicular osteosarcoma as determined by IHC, dogs receiving cytotoxic chemotherapy or who have received cytotoxic chemotherapy within the last 8weeks, clinically significant abnormalities on baseline complete blood count and/or biochemical profile, significant concurrent illness (including autoimmune or immune mediated disease or history of autoimmune or immune mediated disease, significant proteinuria, infectious disease etc., any unregulated chronic disease for which the dog is receiving daily medication. This includes but is not limited to: hyperadrenocorticism, neurologic disease, heart disease, liver disease, and/or renal disease.

Dogs will be monitored for responses to therapy using blood work and thoracic radiographs.

d_sv_content.name: CAR T Cell and Verdinexor Therapy for Treatment of Glioma Tumors in Dogs
d_sv_content.tagline: CAR T Cell and verdinexor Therapy for Treatment of Glioma Tumors in Dogs
d_sv_content.description:
About the study


Every year, about 3 out of every 100 dogs will be diagnosed with a brain tumor. Many of these dogs will be diagnosed with a glioma tumor, which is the second most common type of brain tumor and also, unfortunately, the most difficult to treat. One of the most promising developing areas of research for treating glioma tumors is immunotherapy, which is a type of intervention that uses the dog's own cells to fight the cancer cells.


This study is looking at a specific type of immunotherapy called CAR T cell therapy. CAR T cells are created by doing a simple blood draw from the dog to extract the T cells ("fighter" cells), which are then infused with a Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) protein. This "upgrade" allows the T cells to target and attack the glioma tumor cells. This intervention has been used in children with brain tumors but this study will be the first time it's being used in dogs with glioma tumors!


In addition to the immunotherapy, we will be looking at a specific type of chemotherapy that has shown extremely promising results in canine lymphoma, along with human glioma tumors. This chemotherapy drug, verdinexor, will be used in combination with the CAR T cell therapy in an effort to produce the best possible outcome.


Who qualifies


Dogs who are over 10kg (22lb) in body weight who have already had a brain tumor diagnosed on MRI.

Tumor must be surgically accessible to allow for biopsy and injection of CAR T cells directly into the tumor

Dogs must be healthy enough to safely undergo anesthesia for the biopsy of the tumor

Dogs cannot have previously received chemotherapy or radiation for this tumor


Study activities and Timeline


Visit 1 | Day-17

  1. Exam
  2. Blood draw to create CAR T cells
  3. Begin verdinexor (chemo) therapy twice per week

Visit 2 | Days -4 and -3

  1. On both days, we will give a drug that temporarily depletes the immune system to prepare your dog's body for the CAR T cell injection

Visit 3 | Days 0, 1, and 3

  1. The first day will consist of the first CAR T cell injection while the next 2 days consist of recheck exams

Visit 4 | Days 8 - 10

  1. The visits throughout these days will consist of a brief planning scan followed by the brain biopsy surgery. During the surgery, a second injection of CAR T cells will be given directly into the tumor.

Visit 5 | Month 3

  1. We will do a recheck a MRI to evaluate the tumor response


Verdinexor will continue to be given at home twice weekly until the tumor progresses based on neurological signs or growth seen on MRI.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: Possible reduction of tumor and improvement of neurologic symptoms.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks:
The potential adverse effects of the vaccine or CAR-T cell therapy include local vaccine site reactions (swelling, pain, redness, pruritis), mild anorexia and lethargy for first 24h afterwards, risk of anaphylaxis (rare), and cerebral edema and worsening of neurological signs (unlikely) due to peritumoral inflammation from exuberant response of tumor to immunotherapy. Other possible side-effects from the vaccine and/or CAR T cell treatment include serious inflammation, including fever, low blood pressure, and difficulty breathing, based on human trials.  Occasional neurologic effects from the CAR T cells have been observed in humans.  To date, serious adverse effects from CAR T therapy have not been observed in dogs treated at other institutions.  Your dog will be monitored for 24 hours after the infusion of CAR-T cells to ensure this reaction is not happening. If these adverse effects develop, your dog will be treated with corticosteroids to suppress the inflammation.  


The potential side effects of cyclophosphamide include GI upset (vomiting, diarrhea) and in some rare cases transient but severe bone marrow suppression.  If this bone marrow suppression were to happen, there are bone marrow stimulating drugs that could be administered to hasten bone marrow recovery.


The potential adverse effects of Verdinexor include anorexia, vomiting, diarrhea, weight loss, and lethargy.  More serious adverse events include elevated liver enzymes, cough/dyspnea, thrombocytopenia, anemia, and other blood dyscrasias.
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
1. Dogs must have a brain tumor consistent with a glioma based on MRI
  2. Dogs must weigh over 10kg (22lbs)
  3. Neurological status must be such that the dog is able to walk and stand on its own
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
1. Dogs may not have previously received chemotherapy or radiation for the tumor
  2. Dogs with pre-existing airway conditions or bradycardia will be excluded
d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name:
CAR T Cell Therapy: This is an immunotherapy designed to target the glioma cells. Two injections will be given as part of the clinical trial with the first injection given intravenously and the second injection given directly into the tumor during a brain biopsy.


Verdinexor: This is a chemotherapy agent that has been conditionally approved for use in lymphoma in dogs. This drug will be given twice weekly (Tuesday and Friday) by the owners at home until the dog is removed from the clinical trial due to progression of disease or serious adverse events.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_name: The primary study endpoint is tumor response.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_measure: Tumor response will be based on MRI evaluation of size or change in characteristics of the tumor.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_endpoint:
Dogs will remain in the clinical trial until they experience significant adverse events which may include:

  1. Progression of tumor on MRI scan
  2. Progression of neurological signs due to tumor growth

d_sv_content.name: Electrochemotherapy for Nasal Cancer
d_sv_content.tagline: Nasal Electrochemotherapy
d_sv_content.description:
Nasal Cancers in dogs and cats are uncommon and standard treatment is external beam radiation therapy. Side effects from radiation therapy may sometimes be severe and not every patient will qualify or respond to this therapy. Plus, there are significant delays in accommodating patients for timely radiation therapy treatment due to the paucity of centers and available specialists.


Nasal Electrochemotherapy has been used predominantly outside of the United States (see below).


Radiol Oncol 2017 Nov 1;51(4):422-430.

 doi: 10.1515/raon-2017-0043. eCollection 2017 Dec.

Minimally Invasive Electrochemotherapy Procedure for Treating Nasal Duct Tumors in Dogs using a Single Needle Electrode

Felipe Maglietti 1 2 3, Matías Tellado 4, Nahuel Olaiz 1 2 3, Sebastian Michinski 1 2 3, Guillermo Marshall 1 2 3


Abstract

Background: Nasal cavity tumors are usually diagnosed late, when they already have infiltrated adjacent tissues thus requiring very aggressive treatments with serious side effects. Here we use electrochemotherapy (ECT), a well demonstrated treatment modality for superficial tumors.

Materials and methods: In the case of deep-seated tumors, the main limitation of ECT is reaching the tumor with an appropriate electric field. To overcome this limitation we introduce the single needle electrode (SiNE), a minimally invasive device that can deliver an appropriate electric field with a simple procedure. Twenty-one canine patients with spontaneous tumors were selected, eleven were treated using the SiNE with ECT, and ten with surgery plus adjuvant chemotherapy as a control group.

Results: In the SiNE group, 27% achieved a complete response, 64% had a partial response, and 9% had a stable disease. This means that 91% of objective responses were obtained. The mean overall survival was 16.86 months (4-32 months, median 16.5 months), with a survival rate significantly higher (p = 0.0008) when compared with control group. The only side effect observed was the inflammation of the treated nasal passage, which was controlled with corticosteroid therapy for one week. One year after the treatment, 60% of the canine of the SiNE group vs. 10% of the control group remained alive, and after the 32 months follow-up, the survival rate were 30% and 0%, respectively.

Conclusions: ECT with the SiNE can be safely used in canine to treat nasal tumors with encouraging results.


We now have a nasal electrochemotherapy electrode here in the United States.

After each treatment, the electrode is moved proximally until the entire region of both nasal cavities are treated. Side effects are minimal and patients will go home on 3 days of anti-inflammatory medication. This is an out-patient procedure.

d_sv_content.name: Nanoparticle CRT Combined with High Frequency Ultrasound with or without Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors in Dogs with Advanced Melanoma
d_sv_content.tagline: Immunotherapy and High Frequency Ultrasound in Dogs with Advanced Melanoma
d_sv_content.description: This is a randomized two-arm pilot study comparing dogs with advanced melanoma treated with nanoparticle calreticulin based immunotherapy combined with a focused ultrasound (HIFU) with or without an immune checkpoint inhibitor (anti-PDL-1). We have previously demonstrated that delivering a calreticulin (CRT) expression plasmid via a cationic liposome nanoparticle (CRT-NP) generates an immunostimulatory signal in mice tumors, akin to the immunogenic cell death-associated external cell membrane-bound CRT induced by radiation. CRT is a well-known multifunctional chaperone protein involved in cellular calcium homeostasis and immune modulation. The primary aim of this study is to evaluate local and systemic (abscopal) immune effects of CRT-NP based immunotherapy in combination with HIFU with and without an anti-PDL-1 monoclonal antibody (immune checkpoint inhibitor). Dogs will receive CRT-NP intratumorally once weekly for 4-8 weeks along with HIFU applied weekly to the same tumors. An anti-PDL-1 monoclonal antibody will be administered intravenously every 2 weeks, three days post HIFU treatment. Dogs will undergo baseline comprehensive lab work and urinalysis, which will also be monitored throughout treatment. A baseline CT scan or radiographs will be performed and repeated 12 weeks after the start of treatment to monitor for metastasis/progression of disease. Tumor volume will be measured at each visit along with adverse event reporting at each visit as well according to the VCOG Criteria for Adverse Events v. 2020. Tumor biopsies will be performed to monitor immune modulation, T cell infiltration, myeloid markers, and cytokine response. Dogs with a durable response will be monitored long term every 2-3 months. This study has been approved by the UTSW Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.

d_sv_content.name: Treating Dogs With Glioma Using Radiation and Immunotherapy
d_sv_content.tagline: Glioma Immunotherapy (Nanomedicine) and radiation
d_sv_content.description:
Gliomas are aggressive primary brain tumors that pose significant therapeutic challenges in both human and veterinary medicine. In dogs, gliomas are characterized by locally invasive growth and poor overall survival, even with intervention. Brachycephalic breeds—particularly French Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, and Boxers—are disproportionately affected, suggesting a potential genetic predisposition that remains under investigation.

Current treatment strategies for canine glioma typically involve surgical resection when anatomically feasible, followed by adjuvant radiation therapy. Radiotherapy may also be used as a standalone treatment, delivered through various approaches, including conventionally fractionated protocols or stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT). SRT offers the advantages of high precision, greater tissue sparing, and shorter treatment duration. Despite these interventions, the prognosis remains guarded, with median survival times often not exceeding 12 months.

Canine gliomas share many biological, imaging, and histopathological features with human glioblastoma (GBM), the most common and lethal primary brain tumor in adults. As such, dogs with spontaneous glioma represent a highly relevant veterinary patient population for translational research aimed at improving outcomes in human neuro-oncology. Their natural disease course, intact immune system, and clinically comparable treatment environment make canine models especially valuable for evaluating the efficacy and safety of emerging therapies.

One promising frontier in glioma treatment is immunotherapy. In this study, we investigate the combination of stereotactic radiation therapy with an FDA-approved nanoparticle, previously shown to be safe in dogs. This nanoparticle has demonstrated the ability in rodent models to modulate the tumor immune microenvironment by transforming tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) from an M2 (pro-tumor) to an M1 (anti-tumor) phenotype.

d_sv_content.tagline: CAR neutrophils and Radiation  for Dog's glioma
d_sv_content.description:
Gliomas are aggressive primary brain tumors that present a significant therapeutic challenge in both human and veterinary medicine. In dogs, gliomas are characterized by their locally invasive behavior and limited overall survival, even with intervention. Brachycephalic breeds, particularly French Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, and Boxers, are disproportionately affected, suggesting a potential genetic predisposition that remains under investigation.

Current treatment strategies for canine glioma typically involve surgical resection when anatomically feasible, followed by adjuvant radiation therapy. Radiotherapy can be delivered alone also, through various approaches, including conventionally fractionated protocols or stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT), the latter offering greater precision and tissue sparing and short duration treatments. Despite these interventions, prognosis remains guarded, with median survival times often not exceeding 12 months.

Canine gliomas share many biological, imaging, and histopathological features with human glioblastoma (GBM), the most common and lethal brain tumor in adults. As such, dogs with spontaneous glioma represent a highly relevant veterinary patient population for translational research aimed at improving outcomes in human neuro-oncology. The natural disease progression, intact immune system, and comparable treatment environment make canine models especially valuable in assessing therapeutic efficacy and safety.

One promising frontier in glioma treatment is immunotherapy, particularly the use of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-engineered immune cells. CAR technology involves modifying immune cells to express tumor-targeting receptors, enabling them to recognize and destroy cancer cells with heightened specificity. Notably, CAR-engineered neutrophils have demonstrated the ability to traverse the blood-brain barrier—an essential feature for treating intracranial tumors.

These genetically modified cells showed potential in targeting brain tumors with minimal off-target toxicity. Building upon these encouraging results, our current research proposes to evaluate the combined therapeutic effect of CAR immunotherapy and radiation therapy in dogs diagnosed with glioma. The rationale is to transform the tumor microenvironment through CAR neutrophils, potentially enhancing the efficacy and outcome of radiation therapy. This synergistic approach may not only improve survival in canine patients but also provide critical translational insights for the treatment of glioblastoma in humans.

Dogs will be randomized to receive either CAR-modified cell injection (mod-CAR) or no injection. Baseline assessments will include a physical examination, blood work (CBC and serum chemistry), CT for radiation planning, and MRI if deemed necessary. Radiation will be delivered using an Elekta EVO linear accelerator.

Radiation and mod-CAR therapy will follow one of the three treatment schedules:

  1. Fractionated Radiation Therapy: Dogs will receive 15 radiation fractions every other day (Monday, Wednesday, Friday) under short anesthesia over five weeks. Mod-CAR injections will be administered weekly on Tuesdays for four weeks.
  2. Stereotactic Radiation Therapy (SRT): Dogs will receive three fractions of radiation on alternate days starting Monday of a given week. Mod-CAR will be injected on Tuesday during the radiation week and once again on the Tuesday following the completion of the radiation course.
  3. Pulsar Radiation Therapy Protocol: Dogs will receive Pulsar radiation therapy at a dose of 6–8 Gy every four weeks, for a total of 3 to 5 treatments. The maximum cumulative radiation dose will range from 24 to 35 Gy, depending on the fraction size and tumor response.

Weekly blood work (CBC, serum chemistry, and inflammatory profile) will be performed during the radiation period. A first recheck, including blood work, will occur two weeks after completion of radiation.

MRI evaluations will be repeated every three months for one year. Imaging and follow-up costs will be covered by the study.

d_sv_content.name: Radiation + Targeted Therapy for Bladder Cancer in Dogs
d_sv_content.tagline: New combination treatment for dogs with bladder tumors
d_sv_content.description:
Transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) is the most common form of bladder tumors in dogs. Fractionated radiation therapy is one of the most effective treatment options for this form of tumor, and is typically combined with chemotherapy and an NSAID medication. Lapatinib is a newer therapy that has been used as a single agent for the treatment of dogs with this form of bladder tumor. The goal of this trial is to see if the combination of radiation therapy and lapatinib will be safe and well tolerated in dogs with TCC.


If your dog participates in this study, they will receive oral lapatinib through the course of the approximately 4-month study, as well as oral NSAIDs. 5-7 days after starting these medications, they will also complete 15 daily (M-F) fractions of radiation therapy, which requires daily general anesthesia. Patients will get a urinary ultrasound at the beginning and end of the study, which may require sedation for some patients. They will also receive routine bloodwork throughout the course of the study, as well as blood collection at the beginning of radiation, end of radiation, and the conclusion of the study for study purposes.

Very rarely more severe side effects of radiation can include stricture (narrowing) of the urethra or urinary incontinence. Lapatinib can lead to increases in liver enzyme elevation and kidney values, as well as diarrhea and vomiting. d_sv_content.name: Finding draining lymph nodes for anal gland tumors in dogs using minimally invasive surgery
d_sv_content.tagline: Finding Draining Lymph Nodes in Anal Sac Tumors in Dogs
d_sv_content.description: Anal sac cancers in dogs often spread to other areas of the body. This is called metastasis. Local lymph nodes are a common site for the cancer to spread in dogs with anal sac tumors. Removing lymph nodes with cancer improves outcome. However, assessment of the lymph nodes that drain fluid from a tumor can be challenging. A safe and common test is sentinel lymph node (SLN) mapping. This is where we test the first lymph node(s) that drain fluid from a tumor for cancer cells. It has been used in dogs with anal sac cancer. However, the lymph nodes that drain anal sac tumors are located within the abdomen and pelvis. So far SLN mapping on dogs with anal sac tumors has needed open abdominal surgery. Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) has many reported benefits for patients compared to open abdominal surgery, including smaller incisions, reduced pain, and earlier return to function. This is where small incisions are made for cameras and instruments, and tissue can be removed without making a large incision. We have successfully done SLN mapping for anal sac cancer with MIS techniques in dog cadavers. We want to evaluate these SLN mapping techniques via a MIS approach in dogs with anal sac tumors. We also want to see how this compares to a previously studied method called CT-lymphography that is done before surgery. Our goal is to obtain important cancer care information from SLN mapping, but with the potential benefits of MIS compared to open abdominal surgery.

This study aims to evaluate the safety, effectiveness, and optimal dosage of ⁹⁰Y-NM600 targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) in dogs with PTCL. Our research indicates that targeted RPT can effectively reach tumors, regardless of tumor location.


Please note that this is not a double-masked trial; ALL enrolled patients will receive the targeted RPT.


This funded study (after initial screening) covers the following expenses:

  1. All required examination visits EXCEPT for the initial screening visit.
  2. All laboratory work (CBC, blood chemistry, urinalysis), EXCLUDING the initial lab work needed for initial screening.
  3. Tumor Biopsy
  4. PET-CT scans.
  5. Hospitalization.
  6. All costs related to RPT.
  7. Additionally, up to $1,000 is available to help manage any treatment-related side effects, should they occur.
  8. Please be aware that there is no financial incentive for enrolling your pet in this trial. 


Dogs showing a positive response or stable disease at the day 21 assessment may be eligible for an additional 90Y-NM600 dose.


Dogs with progressive disease will be withdrawn from the study and offered either standard of care chemotherapy (at the clients expense) or treatment discontinuation, based on the client's preference.


Please note that the standard of care chemotherapy is NOT part of the trial.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits:
1. Access to a new radiopharmaceutical therapy that targets lymphoma cells while sparing healthy tissue
  2. This treatment has been safely administered to more than 10 dogs with other solid tumors, with only mild, temporary side effects.
  3. It offers an alternative investigational therapy for PTCL, which often responds poorly to standard chemotherapy and is a uniformly fatal cancer.
  4. Your dog's participation can help improve treatment options for dogs and potentially for humans with this type of cancer.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks: NM600 (non-radioactive drug carrier) was administered to healthy control dogs at doses 30-50 times higher than those planned for this study. These dogs were observed for 21 days after the treatment, with no adverse clinical or laboratory effects noted. Additionally, Y90-NM600 (the therapeutic radioactive version of the NM600 drug carrier) at doses to be investigated have been safely administered to more than 10 dogs with other solid tumors, with only mild, temporary side effects. The medical risks from using Y90-NM600 in dogs with PTCL is theoretically higher with this particular cancer as the cancer cells are more likely to involve the bone marrow which is more sensitive to radiation damage than other organs. This theoretically could lead to increased risk of bone marrow adverse events such as low red blood cell counts (anemia), low white blood cell counts (leukopenia) and low platelet counts (thrombocytopenia) which could result in poor tissue oxygenation, increased risk of infections, and spontaneous bleeding which could be life-threatening and even cause death. Although we do not anticipate such severe adverse reactions from administering 90Y-NM600, dogs will be monitored throughout each hospital stay and clinic visit. This monitoring will include full physical exams and, at specified time points, blood tests, biochemistry profiles, and urinalysis. Owners will also observe their dogs for side effects such as lethargy, vomiting, diarrhea, loss of appetite, respiratory issues, or any behavioral changes after hospital discharge.

d_sv_content.name: Clinical Trial of Trametinib in Dogs with Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)
d_sv_content.tagline: Trametinib clinical trial in dogs with AML
d_sv_content.description:
Dogs can develop a serious blood cancer called acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This disease often gets worse quickly, and there is no standard treatment that reliably helps dogs live longer.

This study is testing a drug called trametinib to see if it may help dogs with AML. Trametinib is a medication used in people to treat some cancers. It works by blocking signals that help cancer cells grow. This drug is experimental for use in dogs with AML, and its safety and effectiveness for this condition are not yet known. In this study, all dogs will receive trametinib along with prednisone, which is commonly used to help dogs with leukemia feel better. About 13 dogs are expected to take part in this study.


Treatment is done with your local oncologist. As part of this study, pets will have the following things done:

• A physical exam by a veterinarian

• Blood tests to check blood counts and organ health

• Urine tests

• A cheek (buccal) swab to collect DNA for future research studies related to leukemia and treatment response

• Regular follow-up visits approximately 1 week and 2 weeks after starting treatment, approximately every 2 weeks through Week 12, and approximately every 4 weeks thereafter while dogs remains on study

• Dogs will take trametinib by mouth once daily at home

• Dogs will also take prednisone as directed by your veterinarian

• tiredness or weakness

• vomiting or diarrhea

• loss of appetite

• changes in blood test results

• high blood pressure or protein in the urine

• In rare cases, side effects could be serious or life-threatening.
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
1. Diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia confirmed by the Clinical Hematopathology Laboratory at CSU
  2. Presence of circulating leukemic cells in peripheral blood sufficient for longitudinal monitoring
  3. Baseline evaluation completed, including physical examination, CBC, serum biochemistry profile, and urinalysis.
  4. Owner willingness to comply with study visits, medication administration, and monitoring.
  5. Dogs must not be too affected by their disease to participate (clinician judgment)
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
1. Concurrent administration of other anti-cancer therapies.
  2. Failure to complete washout period from prior therapy (minimum 1 week for L-asparaginase and 2 weeks for cytotoxic chemotherapy unless clinically justified).
  3. Severe uncontrolled systemic illness that would interfere with study participation or interpretation of outcomes/adverse events.
  4. Any condition deemed by the investigator to create unacceptable risk.

d_sv_content.name: Osteosarcoma- Targeted Bone Electrochemotherapy with Cementoplasty; Alternative to Amputation
d_sv_content.tagline: Osteosarcoma- Targeted Electrochemotherapy of Bone with Cementoplasty
d_sv_content.description:
Canine appendicular osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs. Standard treatment is amputation and chemotherapy with median survival around 13 months. Some patients are not candidates for amputation due to obesity, orthopedic conditions or other mitigating circumstances. Limb sparing is another option but limited in availability and is considered invasive.


Targeted bone electrochemotherapy (ECT-B) is an emerging focused cancer treatment therapy predominantly utilized in people with metastatic cancer to bone as a component of reducing bone pain and retarding tumor growth. It involves the insertion of a single pole electrode into the tumor and drawing chemotherapy directly to the tumor. In addition, once treatment is rendered, the remaining bone defect will be filled via sterile orthopedic bone cement, the patient recovered and discharged the same day.

control of bone pain


extended survival
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks:
Pathologic fracture of bone


Progressive disease


Infection
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
Canine patient with a Diagnosis of Appendicular Osteosarcoma


Overall survival of > 1 month


No concurrent or mitigating diseases
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
Overall survival < 1 month


concurrent or mitigating disease
d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name:
Electroporation, specifically Targeted Electrochemotherapy of Bone (ECT-B)



Targeted Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is a cancer treatment combining chemotherapy (like bleomycin or cisplatin) with electrical pulses. The pulses cause reversible electroporation, temporarily opening pores in cell membranes so drugs enter cancer cells up to 1,000× more effectively. It is highly effective for localized tumors and skin nodules. 


How It Works

Doctors administer a low-dose chemotherapy drug either intravenously or directly into the tumor. Shortly after, an electrode probe is placed on or inserted into the tumor to deliver short, intense electrical pulses. These pulses allow large, normally impermeable chemotherapy molecules to penetrate the cell's interior, destroying the tumor while sparing surrounding healthy tissue.

d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_endpoint: Overall Survival

d_sv_content.name: Developing a Blood Test for Early Detection of Bone Cancer Relapse
d_sv_content.tagline: Developing a Blood Test for Early Detection of Bone Cancer Relapse
d_sv_content.description:
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone cancer in dogs, specially in large size breeds and it presents a high biological aggressiveness, in many cases at the time of diagnosis, metastatic dissemination has already occurred. Currently, the standard of care consists of surgical excision of the affected limb, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. However, despite initial therapeutic response, patients develop treatment resistance, leading to the presence of metastasis, most commonly within the lungs, reducing life expectancy and quality of life of the patient. 

Recently the use of liquid biopsies, a minimally invasive sample collection from body fluids, such as blood, has been increasing, as they detect specific molecular biomarkers. Liquid biopsies can aid in the detection of certain pathologies, monitor disease progression or recurrence after the treatment, the latter can be achieved by measuring molecules such as proteins and microRNAs that are in the circulating blood. These proteins and microRNA might provide less invasive and faster detection than other techniques, such as computerized tomography (CT scan). 

For our research the main goal is to determine if this blood test is able to predict osteosarcoma recurrence, as these biomarkers may provide an earlier status of relapse, and could aid in designing more effective treatments. To support this, our team is developing a lab-on-a-chip platform that can measure the selected biomarkers using a minimal volume of blood. To achieve the previous, we are looking for canine patients, over 25 kg (55.11 lbs) that have been diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma, and have not undergone amputation of the affected limb.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits:
Your dog may not experience direct medical benefit from enrolling. However, the participation of your dog in this clinical study contributes to the advancement of diagnostic and therapeutic protocols for osteosarcoma, with the goal of improving future clinical management of the disease. The knowledge gained from this study may enhance monitoring strategies and follow‑up care for future canine osteosarcoma patients as well as human patients, as osteosarcoma in dogs closely mirrors the disease in children and young adults, the findings may also provide approaches to human osteosarcoma management, potentially benefiting both species.

Enrolled patients will receive additional follow‑up CT scans at no cost, which may facilitate earlier identification of disease recurrence. Early detection does not guarantee improved clinical outcomes, and all decisions regarding treatment will continue to be made exclusively between you and your veterinary care team.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks:
This study does not involve any experimental drugs or treatments. All cancer treatments (surgery and chemotherapy) are standard of care and may be recommended whether or not your dog participates in the study. 

Study-related procedures and associated risks include: 

  1. Blood Collection: 

Small additional blood samples will be collected at the same time as routine blood draws. Potential risks include mild, temporary discomfort, bruising, or swelling at the needle site. These risks are minimal and are managed by trained veterinary staff using standard clinical procedures. 

  1. CT Scans: 

CT scans are part of routine follow-up care for dogs with osteosarcoma and may be performed regardless of study participation. Risks associated with CT imaging may include those related to short-term sedation or anesthesia. With anesthesia there are potential risks, including adverse drug reactions, prolonged recovery or lethargy, vomiting, or more serious complications. These risks will be discussed with you by your veterinary team prior to each scan and are managed according to standard hospital protocols. All drugs and procedures used in this study have been carefully tested to minimize adverse effects. However, your dog may experience unexpected side effects that could be mild or severe. Your animal will closely be monitored for side effects.
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria: This study seeks to enroll dogs with naturally occurring appendicular (limb) osteosarcoma weighing more than 25 kg (55.11 lbs). Eligible patients must not have undergone prior amputation of the affected limb, as collection of pre‑amputation blood samples is required. All enrolled subjects will receive standard‑of‑care management, consisting of surgical amputation of the affected limb followed by postoperative chemotherapy, administered according to the attending veterinarian’s clinical assessment.
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria: The trial will exclude patients whose body weight is less than 25 kg (55.11 lbs), that have been diagnosed with cancers other than osteosarcoma, and/or that have already undergone surgical amputation of the affected limb.
d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name: The study will utilize plasma, from canine patients that have been diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma prior to surgical limb amputation. With the plasma samples the presence of proteins and microRNA enclosed in extracellular vesicles will be assessed to identify potential blood-based biomarkers. In order to determine whether there are changes in the selected protein/microRNA, a serial blood collection at specific timepoints (prior to amputation of the affected limb, 2 weeks post-amputation, and subsequently at 5, 8 and 11 months after amputation) will be taken. Computed Tomography (CT) imaging will also be performed the same day the blood is taken, to assess the presence or absence of metastases. The main objective is to determine what blood-based biomarkers can be used as early indicators of osteosarcoma recurrence, in order to improve the monitoring strategies, as well as to see if that can help predict osteosarcoma recurrence at an earlier stage compared to conventional imaging strategies.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_measure: Obtention of blood from canine patients diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma. The blood will be obtained at the following predefined timepoints during treatment and follow-up. Blood obtention: before the amputation, two weeks after the amputation, 5, 8 and 11 months after amputation, as well as during the chemotherapy treatment visits. With the obtained blood, we’ll search for proteins that can be used as prognostic biomarkers for early recurrence of osteosarcoma.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_endpoint: Obtention of plasma to measure the proteins that can be useful as biomarkers.
d_avma_studycontent_data.sec_outcome1_name: Quantification of the selected biomarkers obtained from plasma, as well as correlating the values with clinical and imaging findings.
d_avma_studycontent_data.sec_outcome1_measure: The measurement of the selected biomarkers will be done by using a developed lab-on-a-chip platform.
d_avma_studycontent_data.sec_outcome1_endpoint: The biomarkers will be compared between the different timepoints they were obtained, as well as with the CT scans imaging results.

d_sv_content.name: Nasal Cancer Treatment with Electrochemotherapy
d_sv_content.tagline: Nasal Cancer Treatment
d_sv_content.description:
Nasal cancer in dogs and cats are uncommon with carcinomas being most common in dogs. Treatment has been limited to external beam radiation therapy at significant expense and often multiple days of anesthesia needed. Median survival is about 1 year and side effects are common. Electrochemotherapy is the use of electrical impulses to open cell membranes driving chemotherapy locally, i.e. a targeted therapy.


We now have an electrode that may be used for nasal tumors based on published material below:.


Radiol Oncol.2017 Nov 1;51(4):422-430. doi: 10.1515/raon-2017-0043. eCollection 2017 Dec. Minimally InvasiveElectrochemotherapyProcedure for TreatingNasalDuct Tumors inDogs using a Single Needle Electrode. Maglietti F,Tellado M,Olaiz N,Michinski S,Marshall G


Nasal cavity tumors are usually diagnosed late, when they already have infiltrated adjacent tissues thus requiring very aggressive treatments with serious side effects. Here we useelectrochemotherapy(ECT), a well demonstrated treatment modality for superficial tumors. MATERIALS AND METHODS:In the case of deep-seated tumors, the main limitation of ECT is reaching the tumor with an appropriate electric field. To overcome this limitation we introduce the single needle electrode (SiNE), a minimally invasive device that can deliver an appropriate electric field with a simple procedure. Twenty-one canine patients with spontaneous tumors were selected, eleven were treated using the SiNE with ECT, and ten with surgery plus adjuvant chemotherapy as a control group.RESULTS:In the SiNE group, 27% achieved a complete response, 64% had a partial response, and 9% had a stable disease. This means that 91% of objective responses were obtained. The mean overall survival was 16.86 months (4-32 months, median 16.5 months), with a survival rate significantly higher (p = 0.0008) when compared with control group. The only side effect observed was the inflammation of the treatednasalpassage, which was controlled with corticosteroid therapy for one week. One year after the treatment, 60% of the canine of the SiNE group vs. 10% of the control group remained alive, and after the 32 months follow-up, the survival rate were 30% and 0%, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: ECT with the SiNE can be safely used in canine to treatnasaltumors with encouraging results. Those clients not electing to participate with this therapy will be followed and data used for comparison. Rechecks may also be done with RDVM but advanced imaging post treatment would be necessary to follow response. While the study is for canine patients, there is no reason not to look at feline and wildlife with the same or similar diagnosis.


The procedure involves a short general anesthesia and is generally an outpatient procedure. Minimal side-effects have been noted and anti-inflammatory pain management may be necessary for a few days post procedure

d_sv_content.name: The Effect of Intravenous Carboplatin on Pain Control in Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma
d_sv_content.tagline: The Effect of Intravenous Carboplatin on Pain Control in Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma
d_sv_content.description:
This study is currently on hold to enrollment due to a national shortage of carboplatin


We know from people and dogs with this type of bone cancer, that the pain associated with the tumor is severe. In people, after they receive their first round of chemotherapy, there is a significant reduction in the pain severity and of course an improvement in quality of life while undergoing treatment. A very important component of treatment in dogs, is ensuring effective pain control. What we dont know is the impact of adding chemotherapy to the pain control plan. This will help us inform current recommendations and the design of future clinical trials. The goal of this study is to determine the effect on lameness, activity and sleep quality in dogs with long bone osteosarcoma after a dose of intravenous carboplatin. Once enrolled, your dog will get a single dose of carboplatin chemotherapy, which is the standard of care drug we use in this disease. Around this treatment we will measure your dogs response to treatment by using an activity monitor placed on a collar, measure the forces going through each leg while walking and ask you to complete a brief survey. This will be repeated weekly for 3 weeks total at which time the study will be complete and your dog will be eligible to undergo any treatment that you would like based on the recommendations from your care team.
