d_sv_content.name: CHOP vs. LOPP chemotherapy as a first line treatment for naïve peripheral T cell lymphoma in dogs
d_sv_content.tagline: CHOP LOPP chemotherapy for lymphoma
d_sv_content.description: Lymphoma comprises approximately 25% of all canine cancers. Up to 40% of these cases are caused by T lymphocytes, known as peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL). The vast majority of lymphoma cases cannot be addressed with surgery and instead warrant chemotherapy. The standard of care chemotherapy protocol for lymphoma is abbreviated CHOP, which stands for the 4 drugs involved. Generally, dogs with PTCL treated with CHOP chemotherapy tend to experience shorter remission durations and overall survival than dogs with diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL). When treated with CHOP chemotherapy, PTCL dogs have a median survival time of 4-9 months while DLBCL dogs have a median survival time of 11-13 months. Previous studies have questioned whether other, non-CHOP protocols may be better suited for dogs with PTCL in hopes of increasing remission and survival times. One protocol that has been repeatedly investigated is LOPP chemotherapy. This protocol uses two of the same drugs as CHOP and two that are different. Recent studies have demonstrated with dogs with PTCL treated with LOPP can experience survival times closer to 11-17 months. While these findings are promising, none of these investigations have had a control arm of dogs receiving CHOP chemotherapy. The purpose of this study is to provide a direct comparison between the outcomes for dogs with peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL) treated with CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. The findings of this study could help veterinarians understand if one protocol is truly superior to the other for dogs with PTCL. In this study, your dog will be randomly selected to receive either CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. At each visit, their lymph node size, blood work, and overall wellbeing will be assessed. Both protocols involve treatments every 7-14 days and take 4-6 months to complete. Following protocol completion, your pet will return once monthly to assess remission status.

Some patients experience GI upset, low white blood cell count, oralopecia. Most side effects are mild and can be managed at home. Rare cases warrant hospitalization. For breeds predisposedto dilated cardiomyopathy, we strongly recommend echocardiogram, as certain drugs can worsen this condition.

Steroids are permitted within 10 days of enrollment, assuming there is still measurable nodal disease. - No major lab work abnormalities that prevent chemotherapy administration. - No evidence of dilated cardiomyopathy, ventricular arrhythmia, or liver failure.

1. No indolent forms of lymphoma, such as T zone lymphoma
  2. Cutaneous lymphoma will not be included

d_sv_content.name: Pilot study evaluating palbociclib in dogs with melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, mammary carcinoma, or anal sac adenocarcinoma
d_sv_content.tagline: Evaluation of palbociclib in tumor-bearing dogs
d_sv_content.description: This is a clinical trial evaluating the use of a new chemotherapy drug, palbociclib, in tumor-bearing drugs with certain cancers. Palbociclib is currently used in humans with breast cancer and other tumors. It has been given to laboratory dogs to report some pharmacokinetic and toxicity data in preclinical trials. The intent of the clinical trial is to measure drug levels in dogs with cancer to determine a recommended prescription dose. We will also describe side effects and, while not a primary endpoint of the study, tumor response.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: Your dog will have access to a new chemotherapy drug. Potential benefits include shrinkage or slowed growth of their tumor. If your dog responds positively to palbociclib, then you may receive up to a 2-month supply of the drug at no cost. You will also receive your dog’s genomic sequencing results free of charge, although these may take up to a few months to process. These results may help guide future treatment options.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks: We will obtain blood and urine samples at each visit, and there is a minor associated risk of bleeding or bruising at the collection site. Palbociclib was studied in healthy dogs with reported side effects included low blood cells, redness or swelling of the ears, hair loss, rash, dry skin, and soft stool. In these trials, side effects were infrequent at the current drug dose and were typically quick to resolve after discontinuation of treatment. It is unknown whether palbociclib will be effective for your dog’s cancer, which means their tumor could progress during treatment.
d_avma_studycontent_data.diagnosis: Melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, mammary carcinoma, or anal sac adenocarcinoma
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
• Must have a diagnosis of melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, mammary carcinoma, or anal sac adenocarcinoma
  • Must have a tumor measuring at least 3 cm in diameter identified on physical exam
  • Must be otherwise healthy as determined by a physical exam and routine blood work
  • Prior treatment with other anti-cancer therapies is allowed, but all dogs must have cancer progression (tumor growth or spread despite treatment) at the time of study enrollment
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
• Dogs that have or have had any other types of cancer, any illness with a life expectancy of less than one-month, abnormal liver function, or those receiving certain drugs that may affect liver function, are excluded.
  • The supervising veterinarian will review your dog’s medications prior to entry into the trial to determine final eligibility.
d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name:
This clinical trial is meant to investigate the use of palbociclib, an oral chemotherapy drug used in people, in dogs with cancer. After enrollment, your dog will undergo anesthesia and have their tumor biopsied. The tumor will not be completely removed, meaning that visible tumor will be left behind. Tumor samples will be submitted for histopathology (to confirm diagnosis) and genomic sequencing (to identify mutations within your dog’s tumor). Your dog will then receive oral palbociclib, a chemotherapy drug, once daily for at least 7 days. You will need to bring your dog to Auburn University 4 times within this 7-day period. Your dog will be dropped off in the morning at the start of treatment and an IV catheter will be placed. We will obtain 6 blood samples (less than 1 teaspoon each) over an 8-hour period to measure drug levels in the blood. Your dog will then return the following morning for 1 additional blood sample. This process will be repeated 7 days in to treatment. Blood work (CBC, chemistry panel) and urine samples (urinanalysis) will be performed 7 days in to treatment to monitor for potential side effects.

If your dog’s tumor grows larger, then you can exit the trial after receiving 7 days of palbociclib. If your dog’s tumor improves with palbociclib, then you have the option to continue the drug for up to 2 months free of charge. If you continue palbociclib, then we will need to see your dog at the Auburn University 4 times to monitor response to treatment and possible side effects. These visits would include blood and urine sample collection.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_name: Pharmacokinetic study evaluating palbociclib levels in the blood
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_measure: Blood draws 7x over a 24-hour period at Day 0 and again on Day 7
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_endpoint: Your dog can either exit the trial after receiving the drug for 7 days, or you can choose to receive the drug free of charge for up to 2 months. You may choose to remove your dog from the study at any time. Auburn veterinarians may remove your dog from the study because of cancer progression, side effects, and/or lack of compliance with the scheduled monitoring and treatment.

d_sv_content.tagline: Palladia Resistance in Mast Cell Tumors
d_sv_content.description: The University of Florida College of Veterinary Medicine is currently recruiting dogs diagnosed with non-resectable cutaneous Mast Cell Tumors (cMCTs) for a clinical research study. The purpose of this trial is to investigate novel biological characteristics associated with toceranib phosphate (Palladia®) resistance in canine cutaneous Mast Cell Tumors (cMCTs).

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: Standard of care is provided, however, this is a sampling study, so there are likely no direct benefits.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks:
According to the previous clinical trials/clinical studies regarding Palladia, the most common side effects included lethargy, gastrointestinal toxicity (nausea, decreased appetite, vomiting, diarrhea), liver enzyme elevations, and hematological
abnormalities. Possible risks associated with the biopsy procedure include sedation,
bleeding, infection, or wound healing complications. If a CT scan is performed, your dog will be under general anesthesia for this procedure. General anesthesia, in very rare cases, can result in death. Everyone involved in your pet’s care will monitor carefully for side effects. The attending veterinarian will prescribe appropriate treatment and/or supportive care if an adverse reaction is observed. Your pet’s veterinarian will discuss possible side effects with you. If your pet experiences anything unusual during the clinical trial, please immediately contact your veterinarian or the Oncology Service.
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria: Any dog that has a confirmed diagnosis of cutaneous mast cell tumor (cMCTs) that is non-resectable and/or cMCTs that are non-eligible for other treatment modalities or whose owners declined other treatment modalities. The clinicians will further discuss eligibility criteria during the evaluation.
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria: Dogs may not enroll in this clinical study if they have received prior chemotherapy or radiation therapy as treatment for their mast cell tumor and may not receive concurrent antineoplastic therapies while enrolled in the study, exceptions may apply. The clinicians will further discuss eligibility criteria during the evaluation.
d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name: Samples will be collected at several intervals throughout the study.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_measure: Evidence of Progressive Disease
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_endpoint: When the patient is showing signs of progressive disease- the last sample is taken and patients have completed the trial

d_sv_content.name: Trametinib for Dogs with Histiocytic Sarcoma
d_sv_content.tagline: Phase II Open-label Non-randomized Multicenter Clinical Trial of Trametinib for Dogs With Histiocytic Sarcoma
d_sv_content.description: The purpose of this research is to investigate a new anti-cancer drug, trametinib, that specifically ‘targets’ growth signals found in cancer cells from companion (pet) dogs. This study will determine the anti-tumor efficacy of trametinib in dogs with histiocytic sarcoma. We will measure and document how much the cancer shrinks upon treatment, and how the drug helps improve the patients’ outcome and life expectancy. Additionally, the study will test whether markers in the genes within the tumor can predict the response from treatment, which in the future can help select those dogs that are more likely to respond positively to treatment. Finally, in a simple blood test we will determine whether effective drug levels are present in the patient.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits:
Our main goal is to find better ways to treat dogs with histiocytic sarcoma in the future, a cancer that lacks good medical options.
Trametinib may be an effective treatment for histiocytic sarcoma, and may help controlling the disease of your dog. However, results from this study will not be available immediately so there may be no direct benefit to patients enrolled. We hope to identify more effective ways to treat and help extending the lifetime of dogs with this devasting disease.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks:
A clinical study of dogs with cancer receiving trametinib has shown that trametinib was safe and
well tolerated. Results from that study provided a reference dosage that will be used in the
present study. The most common side effects are lethargy, gastrointestinal toxicity (nausea, decreased appetite, vomiting, diarrhea), liver enzyme elevations, hematological abnormalities (anemia, decreased hemoglobin), elevated blood pressure and increase protein in the urine. Possible risks associated with the biopsy procedure include sedation, bleeding, infection, or wound healing complications. Everyone involved in your pet’s care will monitor carefully for side effects. If an adverse reaction is observed, the attending veterinarian will prescribe appropriate treatment and/or supportive care, or discontinue the treatment.
Your pet’s veterinarian will discuss possible side effects with you. If your pet experiences anything unusual during the clinical trial, please contact your veterinarian or the Oncology Service right away.
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria: Your dog has been diagnosed with Histiocytic Sarcoma
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria: Dogs without histiocytic sarcoma, dogs without measurable tumors, dogs with a life expectancy of less than four weeks, dogs who have had chemo in the last two weeks or radiation in the last month, or dogs with concurrent relevant malignancy.

d_sv_content.name: Incidence of hypercoagulability and thromboembolism in dogs with surgically treated primary hepatocellular and adrenal neoplasia
d_sv_content.tagline: Primary hepatocellular or adrenal neoplasia
d_sv_content.description:
The goal of this study is to characterize the hemostatic abnormalities in dogs with primary hepatocellular or primary adrenal cancer undergoing surgical removal and to determine when their hypercoagulability (increased tendency for blood to clot) resolves post-operatively. Additionally, we aim to determine the incidence of thromboembolism (blood clots) in hypercoagulable patients diagnosed with primary hepatocellular or primary adrenal cancer following tumor removal.


Dogs with suspected primary hepatocellular or adrenal neoplasia will undergo standard-of-care procedures, including blood work (CBC, chemistry, and PT/PTT) and CT of the abdomen. Upon enrollment, a TEG and fibrinogen level will be obtained before surgery for the study. Dogs will return in 10-14 days for re-check full-body CT and blood work (PCV/TS, TEG, PLT, fibrinogen). Dogs will return in 15-21 days for re-check blood work. Dogs will continue to return for recheck blood work (PCV/TS, TEG, fibrinogen, and PLT) until their hypercoagulability, based on an elevated TEG G-value, resolves.


If a dog remains hypercoagulable at the 10-14 day post-surgery visit, they will be asked to come back for 3 and/or 4-week post-surgery visits until their hypercoagulability resolves. If a dog remains hypercoagulable at the 4-week post-surgery visit, it will present as needed for 6, 8,12, and/or 16-week post-operative visits until their hypercoagulability resolves. If a dog remains hypercoagulable at the 16-week post-operative visit, blood work re-checks will move to a monthly schedule until resolution is achieved. No future visits are required once a dog becomes normocoagulable. No future visits are required, and monthly blood work will discontinue if a dog remains hypercoagulable at 6 months post-operative (day 182).


The study will cover the cost of your dog's pre-operative chest and post-operative abdominal and chest computed tomography (CT) scan. Additionally, the study will cover the cost of each recheck examination fee and the cost of performing blood work (TEG, PCV/TS, platelet count, and fibrinogen) pre-and post-operatively.


Routine blood work (PT/PTT, CBC, chemistry panel, blood type prior to surgery) will not be covered by the study. The study does not cover the cost of your dog's other preoperative workup (primary tumor biopsy/FNA, pre-operative abdominal CT, thoracic radiographs, etc.), primary tumor removal, hospitalization, post-operative care, or additional oncologic care (radiation therapy or chemotherapy). Costs associated with adverse events (including but not limited to hematoma, and incisional complications) are not covered by the study.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: Patients enrolled in this study will receive post-operative monitoring that is beyond the current standard of care.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks: Dogs can develop local irritation or an allergic reaction to the contrast given intravenously for computed tomography. Additionally, dogs could develop a hematoma at the venipuncture site from their blood draw.
d_avma_studycontent_data.diagnosis: Primary hepatocellular or primary adrenal cancer
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
Eligible patients (any breed of dog) must meet all the following:

  1. Greater than 5 kg in weight
  2. Diagnosis of primary hepatic or adrenal cancer.
  3. Dogs hypercoagulable on thromboelastography.
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
1. Less than 5 kg in weight
  2. A histopathological diagnosis not consistent with primary hepatic or adrenal cancer following tumor removal.
  3. Dogs with endocrine disease (Cushing’s).
  4. An active hemoabdomen (blood in the abdomen)
  5. Evidence of hepatic failure.
  6. Evidence of renal disease (azotemia)
  7. Dogs with anemia or thrombocytopenia.
  8. Dogs currently on anti-coagulant therapy.
  9. Dogs not hypercoagulable on thromboelastography.
d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name: Incidence of thromboembolism
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_name: We will be performing thromboelastography (TEG) to measure hemostatic variables associated with coagulation. Additionally, we will measure the following hemostatic variables: packed cell volume, total solids, fibrinogen, and platelet count. In addition to hemostatic variables, we will be performing computed tomography (CT), to record the incidence of thromboembolism.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_measure: We will be performing blood draws and then using blood analyzers to obtain our hemostatic variables. We will determine the incidence of thromboembolism with computed tomography scans of each dog.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_endpoint: To determine the mean day post-operative hypercoagulability resolves. To determine the incidence of thromboembolism in this population of hypercoagulable dogs.

d_sv_content.name: CAR T cell Immunotherapy for Treatment of Metastatic Osteosarcoma in Dogs
d_sv_content.tagline: CAR T cells for Metastatic Osteosarcoma
d_sv_content.description: Osteosarcoma (OS) is a common cancer in dogs. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma that have macroscopic metastases to the lungs. CAR (chimeric antigen receptor) T cells are a modified version of a T cell, a type of immune cell, that alters them so they can target and destroy cancer cells. Dogs have been previously treated with CAR (chimeric antigen receptor) T cells at other institutions and the treatment has been well-tolerated, but the new CAR T cells being evaluated in this trial have not been evaluated in dogs with cancer, though safety studies were done in healthy dogs, without side effects. The goal of this study is to determine the safety and effectiveness of canine CAR T cells, which will be generated by gene modification of your dogs white blood cells, and then infused back into your dog by an intravenous catheter. In order to help the CAR T cells expand in the body more effectively, your dog will also have to be treated with bone marrow suppressing drugs (fludarabine and cyclophosphamide) for 2 days before the CAR T cells are given back. To help increase the effectiveness of the CAR T cells once they are recruited to the tumor tissues, dogs will be treated daily with oral losartan and propranolol before and after CAR T administration.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: Shrinkage/resolution of tumors
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks: CAR T treatment -serious inflammation (including fever, low bloodpressure, and difficulty breathing), neurologic effects. Cyclophosphamide -GI upset (vomiting, diarrhea) and in some rarecases transient but severe bone marrow suppression; losartan - mild lethargy; propranolol - slow heart rate
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
• Weight > 20 kg.
  • Surgical resection of primary (appendicular) tumor via amputation with a histologically confirmed diagnosis of OS.
  • Measurable pulmonary metastatic disease, documentable on thoracic radiographs, with at least one lesion 10 mm in diameter.
  • Adequate organ function: ANC >2000 cells/mL; hematocrit >30%; platelets > 75,000/mL; creatinine < 2x the upper limit of normal; bilirubin 2.5x the upper normal limit. ALT < 2x upper limit.
  • Performance status of either 0 or 1 on Day 0
  • Signed Owner Informed Consent.
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
• Pulmonary metastatic burden, which in the clinician's judgement would preclude surviving > 30 days.
  • Prior chemotherapy without appropriate washout (3 wks carbo, 2 weeks other drugs). Prior therapy with Palladia/losartan or losartan/propranolol allowed.
  • Metastasis to sites other than lungs.
  • Currently receiving any immune modulatory drug therapy including corticosteroids.
  • Concurrent malignancy or other serious systemic disorder incompatible with this study.
  • Patient is on homeopathic/alternative therapies within 1 day of Day 0. Supplements such as chondroitin sulphate, vitamins, essential fatty acids and glucosamine are permitted.

d_sv_content.name: Clinical Testing of Canine T cells Engineered to Target Osteosarcoma and Soft Tissue Sarcoma in Combination with Oral Immunotherapy
d_sv_content.tagline: Novel CAR T cell treatment for Soft Tissue Sarcoma in Dogs
d_sv_content.description:
The purpose of this clinical trial is to evaluate the safety and anti-cancer activity of fibroblast activation protein (FAP) targeted chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells, alone or in combination with orally administered immunotherapy drugs, in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma. FAP is a protein that is expressed on the surface of tumor cell and can be recognized by a T cell. CAR T cells are when a patient’s own cancer fighting white blood cells are modified to express a receptor which binds a specific molecule expressed on the surface of a tumor cell. The two oral immunotherapy drugs being used in combination with FAP CAR T cells (losartan and toceranib [Palladia]) have already been extensively evaluated in a prior trial in dogs with bone cancer and have demonstrated considerable anti-cancer activity, with minimal toxicity. Studies in rodent models of cancer and in vitro in human and canine OS cell lines have indicated that FAP CAR T cells can exert robust killing of canine OS cells and may complement the activities of toceranib and losartan. Therefore, this trial is designed to determine whether FAP CAR T cells are safe alone and in combination with losartan and toceranib, and if losartan and toceranib can improve tumor infiltration of FAP CAR T cells.


At the start of the study, dogs will have blood drawn (~3 ½ tablespoons) to be used for generation of the CAR T cells. Dogs will also be sedated to have a small sample of their tumor taken for study purposes. They will return 10 days later for an exam, bloodwork, and for oral chemotherapy to reduce the number of normal lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell) to maximize the effectiveness of the CAR T cells. A second dose of chemotherapy will be given at home by the owner the following day. Dogs will then return 14 days after the initial visit for an exam, blood and urine tests, blood collection for study purposes, and CAR T cell infusion. The infusion is given over 15 minutes, and then dogs will stay in the hospital until the end of the day for monitoring. Dogs will return 3 and 7 days later for an exam, blood and urine tests, and blood collection for study purposes. Fourteen days after the CAR T infusion, the tumor will be removed surgically. Visits will be required 2 and 6 weeks after surgery for an exam, blood/urine tests, and blood collection for the study. The study is complete after the visit 6 weeks post-surgery (total study duration of 10 weeks).


Some dogs enrolled in the study will receive two oral immune modulating drugs (toceranib and losartan) for the first ~4 weeks of the study. These will be given at home by the owners 1-2 times daily. Owners will know ahead of time whether or not dogs will be receiving these drugs.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: Possible decreased risk of tumor regrowth/metastasis
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks:
FAP CAR T cells have not been previously evaluated in dogs. Because of this, it is possible dogs will have unexpected side-effects which could be mild, moderate, or severe (including death). Possible side effects associated with CAR T cell therapy include fever, systemic inflammation, and acute graft vs. host disease (the CAR T cells attack other organs in your body and not the tumor), and secondary CAR T cell related cancer.  


Blood collection can occasionally cause bleeding at the site of collection (typically the neck), which can be controlled by pressure. Larger volumes of blood collected for the first sample (ie, 50 ml) may occasionally cause transient weakness, and for this reason activity should be minimized for the first few hours after the initial blood collection.


Side effects of chemotherapy include GI upset (vomiting, diarrhea), hair loss, inflammation of the bladder with blood in the urine, and decreased white blood cell (neutrophil) and platelet counts. If significant decreases in white blood cells were to happen, antibiotics would be prescribed in an effort to prevent systemic infection.


Possible risks from sedative administration for tumor biopsy include drowsiness later in the day or short-term mood alteration, but these side effects typically resolve after 8-12 hours.


Possible side effects of toceranib include: GI upset (decreased appetite, diarrhea, vomiting), decreases in the white blood cell count, muscle pain, elevation in liver enzymes, or protein loss in the urine. These symptoms generally go away when treatment with toceranib is stopped. Losartan therapy has been associated with mild lethargy in 10% of dogs treated with high-dose therapy.
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
1. At least 1 year old.
  2. Weight ≥ 11 kg.
  3. Suspected diagnosis of surgically resectable soft tissue sarcoma, at least 2 cm in diameter; can be enrolled without confirmed diagnosis but this must be confirmed histologically at surgical removal.
  4. Adequate organ function: ANC >1000 cells/uL; hematocrit >25%; platelets > 100,000/uL; creatinine < 2.5 mg/dL; bilirubin ≤ 1.5x the upper limit of normal (ULN); ALT ≤ 3x ULN.
  5. Performance status of either 0 or 1 on Day 0, according to the modified ECOG Performance Scheme (Veterinary and Comparative Oncology, 2011).
  6. Signed Owner Informed Consent.
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
1. Prior anti-cancer therapy within 2 weeks.
  2. Any prior immunotherapy.
  3. Evidence of pathologic fracture (osteosarcoma dogs only).
  4. Pregnant or lactating dogs.
  5. Abnormal CNS function suggestive of tumor metastasis to the brain (seizures or dementia of recent onset).
  6. Uncontrolled or recently diagnosed immune-mediated hemolytic anemia or thrombocytopenia.
  7. Dogs with significant cardiovascular disease.
  8. Concurrent immune dysregulation due to an underlying condition (eg, hyperadrenocorticism,diabetes mellitus, renal disease).
  9. Treatment with immune suppressive medications (other than ocular) for any condition.
  10. Concurrent malignancy or other serious systemic disorder incompatible with this study.
  11. Patient is on homeopathic/alternative therapies within 1 day of Day 0. Supplements such as chondroitin sulphate, vitamins, essential fatty acids and glucosamine are permitted.

d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_endpoint: Unacceptable side effects

d_sv_content.name: Canine Liver Tumor Study
d_sv_content.tagline: Canine Liver Tumors
d_sv_content.description:
North Carolina State University College of Veterinary Medicine is currently enrolling canine patients that have 1-2 liver tumors into a clinical trial that is using a new therapy called INSPIRE, which uses electrical pulses to safely destroy the cells within a tumor.


This study has two treatment group:


One group of study applicants should have 1-2 liver tumors measuring between 1-3cm. Potential candidates will come in through the Medical Oncology service at NC State Veterinary hospital for a screening appointment to check eligibility for enrollment. If the patient is eligible for the study and their tumors are eligible for surgical resection, the patients in this group will return one week later for a one time INSPIRE treatment followed by liver lobectomy a week later to remove the tumors.


The second group of study applicants should have 1-2 liver tumors measuring between 1-3cm. Potential candidates will come in through the Medical Oncology service at NC State Veterinary Hospital for a screening appointment to check eligibility for enrollment. If the patient is eligible for the study and the tumors are not eligible for surgical resection, patients will return one week later for a one time INSPIRE treatment. Patients will then be monitored over a 9-month period which includes five recheck appointments, during which patients will receive a CT scan and bloodwork to monitor the tumors.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits:
This study is fully funded, and patients will receive the following:

  1. INSPIRE therapy, which allows for the treatment of tumors that are inoperable due to their location near critical structures such as major blood vessels and the common bile duct.
  2. At each visit patients will receive the following bloodwork: CBC (complete blood count), Chemistry panel, and Troponin levels.
  3. Oncology consultation
  4. Echocardiogram with EKG
  5. Multiple CT (computerized tomography) scans
  6. Liver lobectomy (if applicable) with histology submission
  7. Submission of a FNA (Fine needle aspirate) of the liver tumors with pathology review
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks:
1. During INSPIRE therapy, there is a risk of muscle stimulation, which can be significantly reduced, if not eliminated, by using a paralytic agent during the procedure.
  2. Anesthetic complications, which are significantly reduced by the bloodwork and diagnostics performed prior to a patient undergoing general anesthesia.
  3. Tumor regrowth.
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
1. Owner's must be willing to travel to North Carolina State University for all study related appointments
  2. Patients have 1-2 tumors that are between 1-3cm
  3. Patients must weigh greater than 30lbs
  4. Patients must be overall healthy with no other major health concerns
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
1. Liver tumors that have become cavitated
  2. Metastasis of the liver tumor, as well as other types of cancers
  3. Major heart disease or heart arrhythmia’s
  4. Owners who are unable to accommodate the study schedule
d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name: This clinical trial is investigating a new cancer therapy called INSPIRE (Integrated-Time Nanosecond Pulse Irreversible Electroporation) which uses ultrashort electrical pulses to destroy cancer cells. INSPIRE has been developed to address the clinical short comings of previous pulsed electric field technologies.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_name: The goal of this study is to validate INSPIRE as a safe and effective treatment for inoperable tumors.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_measure: Computed Tomography Scans
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_endpoint:
1. Major decline in patient's health status
  2. When the patient reaches the end of the study

d_sv_content.name: Treating Metastatic Cancer with PD-1 inhibitor and Targeted Immunotherapy
d_sv_content.tagline: Treatment of Metastatic Cancer with Targeted immunotherapy and PD-1 inhibitor
d_sv_content.description:
Metastatic disease prevents a unique clinical setting especially when the patients is still stable. Options are limited for treatment but may include oral and IV chemotherapy options. With the advent of PD-1 inhibitors, we are now looking to combine the inhibitor with either Telomerase or HER2 immunotherapy in combination as the combined therapies should improve response while minimizing adverse effects and battling the cancer through specific mechanisms.


Trends Cancer 2023 Jul;9(7):543-553.

 doi: 10.1016/j.trecan.2023.04.002. Epub 2023 Apr 27.

Immune mechanisms of toxicity from checkpoint inhibitors

S Jennifer Wang 1, Stephanie K Dougan 2, Michael Dougan 3


Abstract

Immunotherapy has changed the treatment landscape for cancer over the past decade. Inhibitors of the immune checkpoint proteins cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen (CTLA)-4, programmed death (PD)-1, and PD ligand 1 (PD-L1) can induce durable remissions in a subset of patients with metastatic disease. However, these treatments can be limited by inflammatory toxicities that can affect any organ system in the body and in some cases can be life threatening. Considerable progress has been made in understanding the drivers of these toxicities as well as effective management strategies. Further research into understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms that drive toxicity will enable better prediction of toxicity and development of optimized therapies for these toxicities that avoid interfering with antitumor immunity. In this review, we discuss our current understanding of the inflammatory toxicities from immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) and propose optimal treatment strategies for these toxicities.


Clinical protocol: Patients will be treated with standard of care anti-PD1 SOP: Administered as an intravenous (IV) infusion over at least 30 minutes either manually or with a constant rate syringe pump. d_sv_content.name: Immunotherapy for canine oral melanoma
d_sv_content.tagline: Novel immunotherapy for canine oral melanoma
d_sv_content.description:
Oral melanoma is a highly aggressive disease with poor outcomes and no effective treatments. Our recent research has shown that a weakened form of the lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) is safe, and can trigger strong anti-tumor effects.


By injecting a small amount of this weakened virus directly into the tumor, we aim to activate the dog's immune system to fight the cancer. Additionally, we will collect and expand immune cells from the tumor, as these cells are more likely to recognize and attack cancer cells. These enhanced immune cells will then be reinfused into the patient to target existing or potential metastatic disease.


To evaluate our therapy, we will first perform a tumor biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and analyze the immune cells already present (Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes). We will then inject the tumor with the weakened virus. One week later, the tumor will be surgically removed, and immune cells from the cancer will be expanded for future use if metastases are present or develop later. After treatment, we will closely monitor the patients through periodic blood tests and imaging (CT scans) every three months.


A small group of dogs (randomly selected) will be the control, and while not receiving the virus injection, they will have their immune cells extracted from the tumor and expanded to be reinfused in case of progressive disease.


Cost of tumor biopsy, two CT imaging sessions, trial-related blood work, the viral reagent and injections, the collection priming and reinjection of the immune cells. Additionally, participating dogs are eligible to receive a $800 post-trial incentive.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: Potential medical benefits include longer clinical remissions after surgical removal of the primary tumor, slowing down or remission of metastatic disease.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks:
Following tumor biopsy: bleeding, infection of tumor, welling, redness, pain, fever, and/or discharge/pus/odor at the biopsy site.

Following virus injection and reinfusion of immune cells: skin rash, fever, lethargy, anaphylaxis.
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
Dogs that are otherwise healthy with localized cytologically or histologically confirmed oral melanoma will be recruited to the study.


Tumors need to be easily accessible to percutaneous injection and needle biopsy.
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
Dogs with a history of immune deficiency or requiring immunosuppressive medications will be excluded.


A dog that received local radiation therapy to the primary tumor before trial enrolment will be excluded.
d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name: Injection of weakened virus to the tumor and transfusion of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_name: The activation of immune cells will be analyzed in the lab using tissues collected from the biopsy and the surgically removed tumor, both before and after the virus injection.  Patients will be monitored for disease progression and response to therapy for dogs with metastatic disease.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_measure:
The activation of immune cells will be examined in tissues collected from both the initial biopsy and the surgically removed tumor.

All patients will undergo CT imaging of the chest and neck lymph nodes to evaluate their response to therapy.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_endpoint: We anticipate that patients receiving this treatment will experience prolonged remission, while dogs with metastatic disease may show a reduction in the size and progression of metastatic tumors.

d_sv_content.name: COSMyc- IT Trial- Canine Oncology Study for Myc Inhibition Tolerability Trial
d_sv_content.tagline: COSMyc-IT Trial- Canine Oncology Study for Myc Inhibition Tolerability Trial
d_sv_content.description:
Myc (a family of transcription factors encompassing c-, N-, and L-Myc) is a pleiotropic, evolutionarily conserved transcription factor. Myc is one of the most frequently amplified oncogenes in most (perhaps all) human cancers (Dang 2012, Whitfield 2017) and often correlates with aggressiveness of the disease (Wolfer 2010; Lee 2015). In breast cancer, Myc is overexpressed in 30–50% of high-grade tumors, is markedly elevated in triple-negative breast cancer and even further elevated in tumors that display a drug-resistant phenotype (Fallah 2017). In non-small cell lung cancer, Myc amplification is found in up to 30% of malignancies (Ahmadzada 2018; Kalkat 2017).


A new novel peptide that inactivates Myc has been developed and is currently in human trials. The goal of this study is to determine the tolerability and feasibility of administering this novel peptide to dogs with cancer to inform future efficacy studies.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: Myc is a commonly mutated protein in cancer cells. Many different types of cancer take advantage of this molecular pathway. Inhibition of this pathway may lead to a reduction in tumor size or improvement of overall condition. However, it is important to note that you dogs may not gain any medical benefit from participating in this study.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks: In studies that have included other mammals, the most common side effects were infusion reactions. This drug will be given as a slow infusion with a couple of premedications to limit these side effects. Other side effects include gastrointestinal upset, lethargy, fever and malaise are also possible.
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
Inclusion Criteria

  1. Any dog with a recent diagnosis of cancer
  2. A cohort expansion of dose level 3 or 4 will be performed for the purposes of pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic end points. These dogs will undergo standard 8 point pharmacokinetic sampling. They will receive additional compensation of $1,000 hospital credit for their participation.
  3. Dogs weighing >10 kg
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
Exclusion Criteria

  1. Dogs that have received chemotherapy (including systemic corticosteroids) within 7 days of study entry
  2. NSAID use is allowable as long as patients have been treated for > 3weeks.
  3. Dogs with any underlying cardiac disease beyond CVDB1 (Chronic valvular disease B1) should be excluded.
  4. Significant hepatic or renal disease (IRIS Stage 2 or higher)
  5. Creatinine > 1.4 mg/dL
  6. Bilirubin > 0.4 mg/dL or ALT > 400 U/L
  7. Modified ECOG performance status >1
  8. No concurrent medications or supplements with anticancer properties
d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name: This is a novel peptide that inactivates Myc inhibiting it's activity in cancer cells where it is commonly over active.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_measure: Adverse events
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_endpoint: The general health of dogs will be measured while they are on this drug for a total of 28 dogs. Physical exams, blood work and owner histories will be used to determine how well the patients tolerate the drug. This drug will enroll 25-30 dogs total until a maximally tolerated dose can be determined.
d_avma_studycontent_data.sec_outcome1_measure: Cytokine panels
d_avma_studycontent_data.sec_outcome1_endpoint: Blood will be taken at regular intevals to determine the activity of the drug in the dog. We will look for increases in certain immune proteins, called cytokines, that may indicate drug activity. In a small subset of 5 dogs we will also take biopsies from the tumor before and after therapy to look for Myc specific inhibition within the cancer cells.

d_sv_content.name: Characterization and Prognostic Evaluation of Infiltrative Immune Cells in Canine Soft Tissue Sarcomas
d_sv_content.tagline: Characterization and Prognostic Evaluation of Infiltrative Immune Cells in Canine Soft Tissue Sarcomas
d_sv_content.description:
The goal of the study is to assess for infiltration of immune cells into tumor samples collected, as well as to monitor for disease progression after surgery. The enrollment will be limited to dogs cytologically diagnosed with soft tissue sarcomas that are at least two centimeters in diameter, undergoing a marginal resection.


Marginal excision of the mass will be performed in all dogs as clinically indicated, following the standards of care. Additional testing, specifically immunohistochemistry, of the tumor sample once removed, will be performed to identify immune cells within the sample. Routine staging post-operatively, as outlined below, will be performed until local recurrence and metastatic disease develop, 24 months of follow-up is reached, or death occurs. Dogs will undergo chest radiographs with sedation given as needed at 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 24 months. If a lymph node is suspected to have metastatic disease or if local recurrence is suspected, a fine needle aspirate of the lymph node or recurrent mass, respectively, will be performed.


The study covers the costs associated with the histopathology of the tumor once removed. Additionally, the study covers the costs of recheck examinations, chest radiographs with associated sedation if needed, and fine needle aspiration of suspected metastatic lymph nodes and local recurrence at 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 24 months post-operatively. The study does not cover the cost of preoperative evaluation, preoperative diagnostics, surgery, and general anesthesia for tumor removal beyond the histopathology charge, hospitalization, post-operative care, diagnostics beyond those outlined above, and additional treatment (such as additional surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy).

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: All patients enrolled in this study will receive current standard of care treatment for a dog undergoing a marginal excision of a soft tissue sarcoma. Dogs participating in the study may not directly benefit from participating; however, the potential information gained from the study may advance diagnostics and treatments of dogs with soft tissue sarcomas in the future.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks: The risks of participating in the study are not beyond those associated with standard of care. General surgical complications for marginal excision of a soft tissue sarcoma and general anesthesia include aspiration pneumonia, drug reactions, hypotension, cardiopulmonary arrest, bleeding, infection, local recurrence, development of metastatic disease, opening of the incision (dehiscence), and need for bandaging. It is possible that enrolled dogs may experience unexpected side effects. It is possible that enrolled dogs' condition may not improve or may worsen. General risks of sedation include systemic reactions such as aspiration pneumonia, adverse drug reactions, hypotension, and cardiopulmonary arrest. Risks of a fine needle aspirate include bleeding, swelling, infection, and nondiagnostic sampling.

  2. Surgery for recurrence or revision of previous definitive surgery

  4. Concurrent diagnosed endocrinopathies

d_sv_content.description: The objective of this study is to investigate the effectiveness of combining doxorubicin and temozolomide with or without propranolol in dogs with hemangiosarcoma. The use of either doxorubicin alone as a treatment for hemangiosarcoma has been studied, and studies with propranolol (historically used to treat heart disease) have shown promise as an added treatment against hemangiosarcoma, however, survival times still remain quite low. A sister drug to Temozolomide, DTIC, has shown promise in improving survival times, however side effects and the long administration times have created challenges with the use of DTIC in dogs. Temozolomide is administered orally and is historically well tolerated in dogs. We are hopeful that survival times can be further improved using a combination approach to treatment, with combination of both intravenous and oral treatments and improved tolerability. Dogs with hemangiosarcoma of the spleen, liver, heart or intramuscular region will be considered for inclusion in this study.

d_sv_content.name: Combinatorial Imaging with PDL1-IRDye800 to Guide Surgical Treatment of Oral Cancer
d_sv_content.tagline: New theragnostic agent (diagnostic and therapeutic) to improve our ability to effectively treat oral cancer!
d_sv_content.description:
Background and purpose


For dogs diagnosed with oral cancer (Squamous Cell Carcinoma, Oral Malignant Melanoma), curative intent surgical removal has been consistently found to have the longest remission rate. However, conventional diagnostic imaging, which we use to plan our surgery, is imperfect and can underestimate the extent of the tumor which results in the potential that not all cancer cells are removed during surgery. This directly impacts patient outcomes (disease free interval and overall survival). There is a critical need to improve our ability to detect cancer intraoperatively (i.e. during the surgery) to improve patient outcomes.


Further, for human head and neck cancer the standard of care is to give immunotherapy (drugs that improve the immune system's ability to fight off cancer) prior to surgery, which has resulted in increased survival in a subset of patients. We have no data on this type of pre-surgical treatment in dogs, and if it would also improve patient survival times.


The purpose of this study is to evaluate the use of a theranostic agent (diagnostic and therapeutic) before surgery to improve our ability to effectively treat oral cancer. This agent is an immunotherapeutic drug (anti-PDL1) bound to a fluorophore. This drug would be given 2X before treatment (surgery or other).


Through this study we will determine if this drug can allow us to see residual cancer cells during surgery (differentiate cancer from healthy tissue) and if treatment of the tumor before surgery with the drug can improve the local anti-tumor immune response (decrease in percent viable cells in the tumor).


If successful this could overall vastly improve our ability to treat oral cancer in dogs.


What happens in this study


  1. An initial screening and eligibility workup, including physical examination, full blood work, urinalysis
  2. A pre-operative biopsy performed at enrollment, to confirm squamous cell carcinoma or melanoma
  3. Intravenous administration of the anti-PDL1-IRDye 800 theranostic probe twice before surgery
  4. Near infrared fluorescence Imaging performed at 8 hours, 24 hours, and 48 hours after probe delivery
  5. Repeat biopsy or curative intent surgery after the second anti-PDL1-IRDye 800 probe administration
  6. Follow-up visits at 7 days and 4 weeks


IACUC: 24708

Study number: VCCT-26-008

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits:
There is currently no non-invasive mechanism for differentiating cancer from normal tissue in real time, which limits our ability to spare healthy tissue and ensure removal of all cancer cells.

It is possible that this therapy may provide a benefit to your dog, but there's no guarantee. Possible benefits include:

  1. ability to differentiate cancer from normal tissue, enabling us to remove all the tumor tissue and improve patient outcomes
  2. immunotherapeutic drug administration (anti-PD-L1) may improve the immune system's response to fight off the cancer
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks:
All medical procedures carry risks, and experimental treatments have the potential for increased risks because they have not been used routinely.

The investigational drug (anti-PD-L1) and the fluorophore (IRDye-800) have been given before to dogs, separately, without side effects. However, anti-PD-L1 bound to IRDye-800 has never been given to dogs before so there is a risk of infusion reaction as well as unknown other side effects, including potentially fatal reactions.

d_sv_content.name: Pilot Study for a New Quasiorganelle Therapy in Dogs with Histiocytic Sarcoma
d_sv_content.tagline: Quasiorganelle therapy for histiocytic sarcoma
d_sv_content.description:
Histiocytic sarcoma is an aggressive cancer in dogs that often does not respond well to standard treatments like chemotherapy or radiation. While some dogs experience benefits, these treatments affect many cells at once and cannot adapt as a tumor changes. New research shows that cancer closely interacts with the immune system and surrounding tissues, suggesting that better treatments may need to work inside cells, not just target them from the outside. Quasiorganelle therapy is an experimental approach that aims to do this by using weakened, non-disease-causing bacteria derived from Listeria monocytogenes to deliver helpful genetic instructions directly into immune and tumor cells, with the goal of improving how the body recognizes and responds to cancer.


The first group (8 dogs) will receive quasiorganelle therapy alone. Their tumor will be measured and they will receive the quasiorganelle infusion. They will then be observed for up 4 days at the MSU Veterinary Medical Center and blood and fecal samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will return for treatment once weekly for 4 doses followed by 2 weeks off. This schedule will then be repeated two more times for a total of 16 weeks of treatment. Imaging to determine alterations in tumor size will be repeated at the end of each 4 week treatment period.

The second group (8 dogs) will receive quaisorganelle therapy that includes gene therapy. Their treatment and monitoring schedule will be identical to that of the first group.

Following the 16 week treatment period, dogs will return for evaluation every 4 weeks or until progressive disease is documented.


Please note: While enrolled, dogs should not live with anyone who is pregnant or planning to become pregnant.

Please note: All treatments and relevant follow up must be performed at Michigan State University College of Veterinary Medicine. Investigational treatment will not be sent to outside clinics.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits:
• Your dog may or may not benefit directly from this study.

• If the therapy works, it could slow down tumor growth or help your dog feel better, but there is no guarantee.

• Your participation may help other dogs in the future and may also help in the development of treatments for humans.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks:
• The therapy uses a weakened form of bacteria. While it is designed to be safe, your dog may experience:

  1.  Fever, fatigue, or mild signs of infection
  2.  An allergic or immune response
  3.  Upset stomach, changes in appetite, or discomfort at the injection site

• If any of these symptoms are apparent, your dog will be treated with medications to manage pain and if more serious symptoms appear they will be treated with antibiotics to eliminate the therapy and excluded from the study.

• Serious side effects are possible but not expected based on earlier safety testing.

• This therapy is not approved by the FDA and is being tested for the first time in dogs with cancer.

• Immunocompromised dogs and humans are the most vulnerable, and thus if there is anyone in your household who is pregnant, on chemotherapy or otherwise immune suppressed, your pet will need to be housed elsewhere, at your expense, until after the therapy is delivered. 

• If you dog has recently been treated with chemotherapy that is immunosuppressive, they will not be allowed to enter this study.
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
1. Confirmed diagnosis of histiocytic sarcoma, including hemophagocytic histiocytic sarcoma, as determined by immune marker expression.
  2. Visible tumor at the time of enrollment.
  3. Up to 5 lesions
  4. Sum of the longest lesion dimensions <15cm
  5. Adequate organ function indicated by standard laboratory tests.
  6. Minimum weight requirement of 20 kg (44 lbs).
  7. VCOG performance status up to 2.
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
1. Concurrent diseases such as: diabetes mellitus, Addison’s disease (hypoadrenocorticism), Cushing’s disease (hyperadrenocorticism), kidney disease
  2. Active wounds.
  3. Concurrent medications such as: immunosuppressants (including corticosteroids, cyclosporine, azathioprine, mycophenolate) or systemic antibiotics within 14 days.
  4. Neutropenia, immunodeficiency, or immune-mediated disease
  5. Prior anti-cancer treatment
  6. Corticosteroid (prednisone) within 7 days.
  7. Chemotherapy within 14 days.
  8. Radiation therapy within 30 days.

The treatment has been tested in laboratory and preclinical studies but not yet in dogs with naturally-occurring cancer. Because animals with cancer may respond differently than healthy animals, this study also looks for early biological or clinical signs that the therapy may be beneficial.

d_sv_content.name: Treatment of Canine Sarcoma with FAP CAR T-cells (FAP CAR-T Study)
d_sv_content.tagline: New treatment with autologous FAP CAR-T cells for sarcomas
d_sv_content.description:
CAR T cell therapy has fundamentally changed how certain cancers are treated. By reprogramming a patient's own T lymphocytes to express a receptor targeting a protein on tumor cells, it directs the immune system to destroy them, producing durable remissions in blood cancers once refractory to conventional treatment.


These benefits have yet to reach veterinary patients, and some cancers remain especially hard to treat with immunotherapy. Sarcomas can be very resistant to standard treatment across many species, including dogs. Led by investigators at Colorado State University, we are testing CAR T cells engineered against FAP, a protein highly expressed in many sarcomas, in pet dogs. We are evaluating both the therapy's activity and its side effects. Advancing this work meets a real clinical need for companion animals while accelerating progress for human patients as well.


In this study, we will test a new treatment for dogs with sarcomas. As the tumor has to be biopsied, this study is best for sarcomas that are external or on the outside of the body.


IACUC: 24677

Study number: VCCT-26-017

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits:
We cannot promise that your pet will benefit from this study. We are still learning if this treatment works. However, possible benefits include:

  1. The tumor might get smaller or respond to treatment
  2. Your pet's symptoms might improve
  3. Your pet might live longer
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks:
This treatment is experimental. The FDA has not approved it. We cannot promise it will work or be safe.

  1. Risks from the tumor biopsy: These risks are uncommon but may include:
  2. pain or discomfort at the biopsy site (common, usually mild and managed with pain medication)
  3. Infection at the biopsy site (uncommon)
  4. Bleeding or bruising (uncommon)
  5. Broken bone at the biopsy site for bone tumors (rare)
  6. Complications from sedation or anesthesia, including allergic reaction or, very rarely, death (rare, estimated <1% in healthy dogs)
  7. Risks from chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide) given prior to CAR T-cell therapy:
  8. Upset stomach, vomiting, or decreased appetite (common, usually mild and self-limiting)
  9. Low blood cell counts, which could increase risk of bleeding or infection (common but expected to be mild)
  10. Sterile hemorrhagic cystitis (bladder irritation causing bloody urine) (uncommon)
  11. Severe infection due to low white blood cell counts, which may need hospitalization and can rarely result in death
  12. Risks from CAR T-cell infusion: Please note: CAR T-cell therapy has been studied in dogs, but CAR T-cells targeting FAP specifically have not been extensively tested. Five dogs have been enrolled so far at other vet schools (Colorado State University and Tufts Vet School) and tolerated the treatment without significant side effects. Because this is a new treatment, there may be unknown risks.
  13. Fever (common in human patients, expected to be manageable)
  14. Cytokine release syndrome (CRS): an inflammatory response that can cause fever, low blood pressure, and difficulty breathing. In humans, CRS ranges from mild (common) to severe (uncommon). Severe CRS can be life-threatening but is treatable if caught early.
  15. Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS): neurological symptoms such as confusion, tremors, or seizures (rare in humans, unknown frequency in dogs)
  16. "On-target, off-tumor" effects: the CAR T-cells might attack healthy tissues that express FAP (unknown risk)
  17. Secondary malignancy: very rarely, CAR T-cells themselves could become cancerous (very rare, reported in humans)
  18. Infusion reactions such as hives, itching, or vomiting (uncommon, usually mild)


How complications will be addressed:

All study-related side effects will be treated by the veterinary team at UC Davis Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital. Your dog will be closely monitored throughout the study, including hourly monitoring on the day of CAR T-cell infusion. If any problems arise, the study team will provide prompt medical care. However, some problems could be serious enough to cause death.


The study will pay up to $2,500 for treatment of study-related side effects. This coverage applies only to treatment at UC Davis. Costs exceeding $2,500, or treatment obtained elsewhere, are the owner's responsibility.
d_avma_studycontent_data.diagnosis: sarcoma, soft tissue sarcoma, FAP CAR T-cells
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
In order to be eligible for trial participation, the subject must:

  1. Be at least 1 year old
  2. Weigh at least 11 kg
  3. Have a histologically confirmed or cytologically suspected diagnosis of sarcoma on the outside of the body
  4. Be free of lung metastatic disease or other significant pulmonary pathology on thoracic radiographs- check with study PI, early metastasis ok.
  5. Have a 2-week washout from prior chemotherapy or other anti-cancer therapy
  6. Have adequate organ function
  7. Performance status 0 or 1 on Day 0 (modified ECOG)
  8. Have written, informed owner consent prior to enrollment
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
The presence of any one of the following would result in the dog being excluded from entry into the study:

  1. Chemotherapy or bisphosphonates within 2 weeks of Day 0
  2. Prior immunotherapy (check with PI, 2-3 week washout ok for Apoquel, Atopica, etc.).
  3. Concurrent malignancy, or other serious systemic disease incompatible with this study
  4. Uncontrolled or recently diagnosed immune-mediated disease (e.g., IMHA, IMTP), or any condition or medication that might affect immune system function
  5. Homeopathic/alternative therapies for their cancer (must be discontinued on Day -1)
d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name:
This new treatment uses special cells called CAR T cells, prepared as follows:

  1. We take immune cells (T cells) that fight disease in your dog's body with a blood draw
  2. We change these cells in a lab so they can find and attack cells that support the tumor's growth
  3. We give your dog oral chemotherapy (Cytoxan) over two days to reduce their natural population of immune cells
  4. We give these improved cells back to your dog through an infusion directly into the blood stream.


The changed T cells are released into the body and will search and kill special cells that help tumors grow called fibroblasts. By attacking these support cells, the treatment aims to damage the tumor's ability to grow and spread and help fight the cancer.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_name: Safety of FAP CAR-T cells administration. Tumor infiltration of FAP CAR-T cells.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_measure: Adverse events, physical examination, blood pressure, laboratory test values, and biocorrelative samples for quantification of CAR T-cell infiltration and persistence.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_endpoint:
The objective of this study is to determine whether FAP CAR T cells are safe for surgically resectable soft tissue sarcoma.

Outcome measures are:

  1. Adverse events (VCOG-CTCAE v2, with specific attention to CRS and ICANS)
  2. Physical examination
  3. Blood pressure
  4. Laboratory test values (CBC, chemistry, UA/UPC)
  5. Biocorrelative samples (PBMC, plasma, and fresh tumor tissue from Day -14 biopsy and Day 14 surgical resection) for quantification of CAR T-cell infiltration and persistence.

d_sv_content.name: Targeted Electrochemotherapy (ECT) Cancer Treatment
d_sv_content.tagline: Targeted Electrochemotherapy
d_sv_content.description:
Targeted Electrochemotherapy (ECT) treatment consists of delivering a low dose of chemotherapy, followed by short electric pulses to the cancer. With the delivery of the electric pulses, cell membranes are transiently opened allowing chemotherapy directly into the cell. Treatment may be repeated over the course of weeks or months to achieve regression of large lesions. Targeted Electrochemotherapy employs lower dosages of chemotherapeutic drugs than standard chemotherapy protocols. In the clinical use of electrochemotherapy, side effects are uncommon and patients maintain or improve quality of life. Currently, Electrochemotherapy in animals is under a short anesthesia and with a variety of electrodes available to us, many tumor types and locations (including internal cancers) are candidates for this therapy.


Targeted Electrochemotherapy, in veterinary oncology (dogs, cats, exotics and horses), has been dominated by centers in Europe and South America. Here at Veterinary Oncology Services, there is not a location where cancer may not be treated. It may be used for a wide variety of tumors including:


Sarcomas in the mouth, eyelid, foot pad, skin or distal limb and their scars, Feline vaccine-associated fibrosarcoma before and after surgery, Melanoma in the mouth, eyelid or foot pad, Squamous cell carcinoma in mouth, eyelid, ear, nasal planum or foot pad, Incompletely resected soft tissue sarcomas where aggressive surgical treatment would necessitate amputation, Localized cutaneous lymphoma in dogs or cats, Local control of mast cell tumors including scars, Perianal & rectal tumors, prostate, pancreas, Hepatocellular carcinomas/adenomas, Perianal tumors, Sarcoids, sarcoma and squamous cell carcinomas in horses, Superficial tumors on exotics (small mammals, birds & zoo animals) If you have a patient that may benefit from this therapy, please do not hesitate to contact us at 845 205 2768 or info@petcancerinformation.com. Please visit our website at www.petcancerinformation.com

d_sv_content.name: Combination of electrochemotherapy and gene therapy with canine IL-12
d_sv_content.tagline: Electrochemotherapy and IL-12 for primary tumors and metastatic tumors
d_sv_content.description:
Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is an advanced treatment in veterinary oncology. It has been routinely used in dogs for treating mast cell tumors, carcinomas and soft tissue sarcomas, in cats for SCC, carcinomas and sarcomas and in horses for sarcoid tumors. ECT is a local ablative technique which has a good local anti-tumor control in dogs (up to 70%) and in cats (up to 80%) and in horses up to 100% but limited impact on distant tumors and metastasis. Therefore, there is a need for a combination therapy which could provide local control with a systemic effect to battle cancer spread. Interleukin 12 is a potent immune stimulator that works by increasing IFN gamma which has an anti-tumor effects through the activation of cytotoxic cells such as natural killer cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes. IL-12 also up-regulates antigen presenting cells making the tumor cells recognizable to the immune system. Several clinical studies have already been performed treating different canine tumors by electro-genetransfer with a plasmid encoding IL-12. Results showed increased systemic IL-12 and IFN gamma with an effect on distant metastasis .

Procedure: The treatment consists of electrochemotherapy with bleomycin (intravenously) and gene-electrotransfer (GET) of IL-12 (intra-lesional). The treatment will be performed in patients under a short general anesthesia. Depending on the tumor volume and the response the treatments will be repeated every 3-4 weeks. Responses will be followed with physical exam and imaging (X-rays or CT). Electrochemotherapy will be performed using direct intra-tumoral application of IL-12 (2mg per patient) and the intravenous application of bleomycin (standard dose). The study is based on multiple publications showing benefit with this combination with control of the cancer including metastasis and minimal to no adverse effects to the patients.


References: 1. Pavlin, D. et al. Electrogene therapy with interleukin-12 in canine mast cell tumors. Radiol Oncol 45, 3139 (2011). 2.Tozon, N., Pavlin, D., Sersa, G., Dolinsek, T. & Cemazar, M. Electrochemotherapy with intravenous bleomycin injection: an observational study in superficial squamous cell carcinoma in cats. J. Feline Med. Surg. 16, 291299 (2014). 3.Tamzali, Y. et al. Successful treatment of equine sarcoids with cisplatin electrochemotherapy: a retrospective study of 48 cases. Equine Vet J 44, 214220 (2012). 4.Reed, S. D. et al. Bleomycin/interleukin-12 electrochemogene therapy for treating naturally occurring spontaneous neoplasms in dogs. Cancer Gene Ther. 17, 45764 (2010). 5.Cutrera, J., Torrero, M., Shiomitsu, K., Mauldin, N. & Li, S. Intratumoral bleomycin and IL-12 electrochemogenetherapy for treating head and neck tumors in dogs. Methods Mol Biol 423, 319325 (2008). 6.Cemazar, M. et al. Efficacy and safety of electrochemotherapy combined with peritumoral IL-12 gene electrotransfer of canine mast cell tumours. Vet. Comp. Oncol. (2016). doi:10.1111/vco.12208

d_sv_content.name: Probiome Trial: Can probiotics improve outcomes in canine bladder cancer?
d_sv_content.tagline: Probiome Trial for dogs with Bladder Cancer
d_sv_content.description: The purpose of this study is to determine if the addition of a probiotic (Escherichia coli Nissle 1917) can improve clinical outcomes when paired with a standard-of-care therapy (vinblastine / piroxicam) for canine bladder cancer - also known as urothelial carcinoma or transitional cell carcinoma (TCC). We will evaluate tumor response, clinical side effects, and quality of life as part of this study. Additionally, we will evaluate immune response and characterize the stool and urine microbiome and metabolome to understand the potential effects of the probiotic. Our broader goal is to improve cancer care and outcomes in dogs with bladder cancer.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: Based on previous studies in humans and dogs, this probiotic is safe and well tolerated in dogs. The probiotic may improve clinical outcomes. For example, dogs receiving the probiotic may experience reduced clinical signs associated with chemotherapy or disease. However, it is also possible that the probiotic will have no effect or a negative effect on a dogs clinical outcomes.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks: Dogs may experience side effects from medications used in this study to treat cancer including vinblastine, piroxicam, or the probiotic. Side effects can include neutropenia, allergic reaction, fever, vomiting, diarrhea, gastric ulceration, kidney damage, lethargy, and inappetence. Disease progression may result in additional clinical signs including lower urinary tract signs or infections.

  4. Female dogs must weigh at least 6kg for inclusion.

  7. Complete blood count and serum chemistry without clinically significant abnormalities, as determined by the veterinarian.

d_sv_content.name: Exploring a Nonoparticle-enabled Treatment of Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Cats
d_sv_content.tagline: Exploring a Nanoparticle-enabled Treatment of Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Cats
d_sv_content.description:
For veterinary patients, surgery is the primary treatment for many tumour types. Surgery may not always be the best option for cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma (OCSCC) as it is challenging to obtain adequate clear surgical margins and often, the disease reoccurs. Adjuvant therapies including chemotherapy, radiation therapy and palliative options are ineffective or poorly tolerated and do not improve the overall survival rate of cats with OCSCC. We need to make improvements to staging and treatment.

PORPHYSOMES (pPs) are a novel nanomedicine developed and supplied by Professor Dr Gang Zheng’s Laboratory (University Health Network, Toronto). These particles are delivered intravenously (in a local vein through a catheter) and concentrate in areas with tumour cells (either the primary tumour location or where the cancer has spread (metastatic site). pPs can be used to highlight the tumour by using a specialized technique called near-infrared fluorescence imaging (NIRF). This equipment allows for image-guided surgery, tumour margin assessment and lymph node staging. pPs can also be used to in combination with photoablation – photodynamic therapy (PDT) to deliver treatment directly to the tumour. 

 

pPs-enabled therapies can have an immediate impact on cancer management providing better patient outcomes. This study offers a novel approach to the treatment of OCSCC in cats. The use of pPs is ground-breaking translational research and the information gained will be used to treat future dogs, cats and humans with cancer. A human clinical trial is planned to be conducted in 2024.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: At this time, we do not know if this therapy will result in an improvement in your cats tumour but we are hopeful there will be benefit. In addition, even without visible improvement there may be some analgesic (pain) effects. Your cat’s and your participation are also an important opportunity to help both future pets and humans. By participating in this study, your cat will help to develop protocols to better diagnose and treat cats and dogs with tumours in the future. Because of the translational element of this work, your cat will also be involved in the validation of this therapy for use in human medicine. The study team is working closely with human clinicians and will be running this study in parallel with a human trial. The results of this study will be published and made available for the benefit of the scientific community. With this scientific publication, neither you, nor your cat, will be identified.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks:
In the proposed study, your cat will undergo two general anesthesia events (CT or MRI and Photodynamic laser therapy). With any anesthesia, there are potential risks including adverse drug reaction, prolonged recovery, regurgitation, vomiting, aspiration, hypothermia, hypotension, tracheal tear, cardiovascular collapse, and death. 

 

We do not expect any long-term side effects for any part of this study but as this is a new agent, there potential risks, both anticipated and unanticipated. Porphysomes have been studied in non-patient cats for tolerability and toxicity. At higher doses (10mg/kg), there were transient blood changes (increased muscle enzyme (CK), increased lipids and white blood cell counts). Health Canada has authorized an Experimental Studies Certificate (PORPHYSOME SOLUTION; DSTS Sub. No: 279878) to conduct this study in client-owned cats.  

  

There may be some drugs that interact with the Porphysome treatment that may cause increased sensitivity to light or make your cat bleed more readily. It is essential to discuss all medications or supplements your cat is taking with the study team. While not documented in cats, it is possible your cat may have an allergic (hypersensitivity) reaction to the lipid in the particles. If this occurs, your cat will be given a steroid or antihistamine. Hypersensitivity effects are not expected to continue >6 hours after administration and are mild and self-limiting. 

  

Some cats may experience skin photosensitivity following the pPs infusion and there is a risk of retinal damage with direct and bright light exposure. Please do not allow your cat to lounge/ sleep in the direct sunlight when inside and avoid outdoor sunlight exposure for periods lasting longer than 30 minutes for at least 7 days following surgery. Specialized eyewear will be provided for your cat (if they will tolerate wearing them), but it is not necessary. If there any concerns, please immediately contact the research team.
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
This study is recruiting cats with naturally occurring oral squamous cell carcinoma. The inclusion criteria for this study are quite broad; the study clinician will go over your pet’s history and medical records to determine their eligibility. 

To be eligible for this study, your cat must have a confirmed diagnosis of an oral squamous cell carcinoma tumour. Testing (fine needle aspirate and cytology +/histopathology) should be completed prior to enrollment. Chest radiographs will also be requiered prior to the study.
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria: Your pet will be ineligible for the study if your cat is anemic, and/or if there has been a previous history of adverse reactions to lipid-based drugs, liver dysfunction or hypersensitivity to iodine, previous chemotherapeutic treatment for oral squamous cell carcinoma tumour and/or active disease unrelated to the tumour.
d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name: This trial involves the use of porphysomes and photodynamic laser therapy to accurratly confirm there are no side effects of the porphysomes being studied. This trial also explores the efficacy of the porphysomes as a diagnostic method for metastasis and to evaluate the effect of progression of porphysome medicated photodynamic laser therapy in cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma to deterime the treatment efficacy.

d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_measure: Blood and urine will be collected for routine evaluation and for evaluation to response to the porphsyome infusion. Tumour will be collected for evaluation of porphysome distribution in the tumour as well as level of necrosis in the tumour after photodynamic therapy. A Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and/or c scan

d_sv_content.name: Dual Energy CT to Assess Bone Mineral Density in Dogs with Osteosarcoma Undergoing Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy
d_sv_content.tagline: Changes in Bone Density Following Radiation Treatment in Dogs with Osteosarcoma
d_sv_content.description:
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs and, while amputation followed by systemic chemotherapy is the standard of care, it may not be the most appropriate treatment option for all dogs or it may not meet the goals of individual owners. Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) has been utilized to kill tumor cells while leaving the affected limb intact showing good primary tumor control rates. The biggest risk with using SBRT in this setting is the potential for pathologic fracture of the affected limb. Here we plan to use a dual energy CT for radiation planning and to quantify bone mineral density (BMD) both before and after SBRT to assess changes that happen with SBRT treatment. BMD measures calcium and other minerals. In theory, the more mineral, the denser and stronger the bone is and less likely it is to break. In addition, we will measure bone breakdown markers before and after treatment to determine how these are correlated with the BMD and response to treatment.


Once enrolled, dogs will have blood and urine collected for bone breakdown markers followed by 3 doses (or fractions) of SBRT. On the third and final fraction, dogs will receive the first dose of standard of care chemotherapy (carboplatin). Two weeks after chemotherapy, your dog will need to have a complete blood count performed to assess response to chemotherapy as well as blood and urine collected for the bone breakdown markers. At each dose of chemotherapy, a total of 6, blood and urine will be collected to assess trends in these markers. At the time of the final chemotherapy treatment, an additional dual energy CT will be performed to assess the changes that happen to the bone after treatment. Once chemotherapy is complete, it is recommended that your dog return every 8 weeks for chest x-rays; blood and urine will be collected for the study at the 1st 3 visits post-chemotherapy. At any change in lameness or concern for progression of disease, it is expected that your dog will return to CSU for assessment and evaluation of the bone markers.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: Likely none related to study participation specifically; SBRT is usually associated with reduction/resolution of pain from bone tumor and reduction/elimination of local disease progression, and carboplatin with delay/prevention of metastatic disease
