d_sv_content.name: Dose escalation study for a novel STING agonist in tumor-bearing dogs
d_sv_content.tagline: Dose escalation study for a novel STING agonist in tumor-bearing dogs
d_sv_content.description:
Immunotherapy, engaging the power of the immune system against cancer, has become a standard part of oncology care. One such approach utilizes the STimulator of INterferon Genes (STING) pathway. Our colleagues at University of Michigan, led by Dr. James Moon, have developed a drug that activates the STING pathway. This drug, called CMP-002, has been shown to combat cancer in a laboratory setting, with and without the use of another modulator of immune system, PD-1 blockade. This success prompted a collaboration with Michigan State University College of Veterinary Medicine as we hope to contribute to efforts that can help veterinary oncology patients and humans alike. Our initial studies, led by Dr. Vilma Yuzbasiyan-Gurkan at MSU, established the dose range tolerated in healthy dogs.

The purpose of this study is to confirm the best dose of CMP-002 with or without PD-1 blockade for tumor-bearing dogs. CMP-002 has already been tested in healthy dogs. It is not uncommon for patients with cancer to process drugs differently, which is why we intend to confirm the best dose for tumor-bearing dogs. The findings of this study will then be used in future studies assessing the anti-cancer properties of CMP-002 with or without PD-1 blockade.


There will be two study groups:


The first group of patients (6–9 dogs) will receive CMP-002 alone. Their tumor will be measured and they will receive the CMP-002 infusion. They will then be observed overnight and blood samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will visit their primary veterinarians one week later for blood sampling. Three weeks after the first treatment, the dogs will return to the MSU Veterinary Medical Center for a second infusion. Depending on previous response, they may be hospitalized again or sent home the same day. If tolerated, these treatments can be repeated every 3 weeks for a set number of cycles. Tumor biopsy samples may be collected at various timepoints.


The second group of dogs (6–9 dogs) will receive CMP-002 with PD-1 blockade. Their tumor will measured and they will receive the CMP-002 infusion. They will then be observed overnight and blood samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will return one week later for tumor measurements, blood sampling, and anti-PD-1 infusion. Three weeks after the first treatment, the dogs will return to the MSU Veterinary Medical Center for a second CMP-002 infusion. Depending on previous response, they may be hospitalized again or sent home the same day. If tolerated, these treatments can be repeated every 3 weeks for a set number of cycles. Tumor biopsy samples may be collected at various timepoints.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits:
1. This treatment uses immunotherapy, stimulating the immune system to kill cancer cells. Other forms of standard of care cancer treatment include surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy. While effective, none of these treatments seek to harness the body’s own power to combat cancer.
  2. All study visits must be through MSU-CVM, while non-study dogs may do some treatments with their primary veterinarian.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks:
While significant test compound toxicity or adverse effects are not anticipated or intended, the design of the studies themselves include monitoring of clinical signs. Additionally, the rising dose design allows the option of not increasing to a higher dose and/or discontinuation of dosing if indicated by clinical or laboratory findings.


An anaphylactic reaction was observed in a previous tolerability study in one dog in the IV bolus administration, we do not expect this to be the case with the slow IV infusion. The most recent tolerability study in purpose-bred dogs showed that slow infusion over 30 minutes improved tolerability. However, the veterinary staff will be ready to intervene should such a reaction develop.

Adverse effects noted in the recent tolerability study included fever, shivering, nausea and vomiting.

d_sv_content.name: Mammary tumors in cats
d_sv_content.tagline: Polarization sensitive optical coherence tomography for surgical margin assessment for mammary tumors
d_sv_content.description:
Surgery is the most common treatment used for mammary cancer in cats. The pathologist determines whether surgery has removed all cancer cells many days after the procedure. We need rapid and accurate testing during surgery to detect residual cancer to decrease cancer recurrence and the necessity for repeated surgery or treatments.


Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is an imaging technology that uses near-infrared light waves to generate real-time, high-resolution images of the microscopic structure of tissues, specifically looking at the organization of the tissues. We have performed some initial evaluations using this optical coherence tomography for detection of residual cancer, which has had very encouraging results.


Cats will undergo surgery to remove their tumor; following removal, the tumor will be scanned with polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography to assess the surgical margins for residual cancer cells. The specimen will then undergo thorough histopathological assessment.


The overall purpose of the study is to evaluate a new imaging method to detect cancer cells left behind following removal of mammary tumors in client-owned cats undergoing surgery. This technology has been used successfully in human breast cancer surgery, providing microscopic assessment of surgical margins within minutes. Identifying a rapid and thorough imaging method to detect any remaining cancer cells during surgery for mammary tumors will support targeted treatment management decisions and improve outcomes for cats and dogs with cancer.


Pet owners are financially responsible for all costs associated with evaluation and surgery. Each pet owner receiving surgery at OSU will receive a $70 credit to their account to cover the costs of the histopathology evaluation.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: This research will open the door to veterinarians having the technology to allow accurate real-time interpretation of surgical margins to minimize the necessity for additional surgeries or other treatments and decrease tumor recurrence.

  1. Have cytology or histopathology confirmation of a mammary tumor
  2. Undergo surgical excision of a mammary tumor at OSU

d_sv_content.name: Electrochemotherapy for Bone Cancer
d_sv_content.tagline: Electrochemotherapy for Bone cancers
d_sv_content.description:
Electrochemotherapy is a valuable anti-cancer therapy in both human and veterinary patients. Until recently, there was no electrode to allow treatment of bone lesions. Veterinary Oncology Services (www.petcancerinformation.com) has a bone electrode used in human applications (see below).


Curr Oncol. 2022 Mar 4;29(3):1672-1682. doi: 10.3390/curroncol29030139.

Electrochemotherapy Is Effective in the Treatment of Bone Metastases

Laura Campanacci 1, Luca Cevolani 1, Francesca De Terlizzi 2, Laura Saenz 3, Nikolin Alì 1, Giuseppe Bianchi 1, Davide Maria Donati 1


Abstract

Bone metastases induce pain, risk of fracture, and neural compression, and reduced mobility and quality of life. Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is a minimally invasive local treatment based on a high-voltage electric pulse combined with an anticancer drug. Preclinical and clinical studies have supported the use of ECT in patients with metastatic bone disease, demonstrating that it does not damage the mineral structure of the bone and its regenerative capacity, and that is feasible and efficient for the treatment of bone metastases. Since 2009, 88 patients with bone metastasis have received ECT at the Rizzoli Institute. 2014 saw the start of a registry of patients with bone metastases treated with ECT, whose data are recorded in a shared database. We share the Rizzoli Institute experience of 38 patients treated with ECT for a bone metastasis, excluding patients not included in the registry (before 2014) and those treated with bone fixation. Mean follow-up was 2 months (1-52). Response to treatment using RECIST criteria was 29% objective responses, 59% stable disease, and 16% progressive disease. Using PERCIST, the response was 36% OR, 14% SD, and 50% PD with no significant differences between the two criteria. A significant decrease in pain and better quality of life was observed at follow up.


Clinical protocol: Patient will be anesthetized and the lytic area of bone to be treated identified. Using a Jamshidi bone needle, a core will be created allowing placement of the linear bone electrode into the lesion. Once in place, targeted electrochemotherapy will be applied into the lytic lesion. Bleomycin will be injected IV and after 8 minutes the pulse will be sent into the bone lesion allowing a transient opening of the cell membrane. 2- 3 treatments will be completed and the area wrapped upon recovery.


Follow up imaging in 4 and 8 weeks with radiographs.

d_sv_content.tagline: Evaluation of Weekly Intratumoral Cowpea Mosaic Virus in Dogs with Solid Tumors.
d_sv_content.description: This is an open-label, pilot study evaluating the safety and preliminary efficacy of Cowpea Mosaic Virus (CPMV) administered as an intratumoral injection in dogs with mast cell tumor, soft tissue sarcoma, melanoma, and thyroid tumors. CPMV will be administered as an injection into the tumor once weekly for 4 weeks. If there is >/= 25% reduction in tumor size, an additional 4 doses may be administered for a total of 8 doses. Dogs may have their tumors removed at the end of the initial 4 treatments or after 8 treatments. Hepatic and renal function tests will be monitored on the first day, at day 7 and 2,4, 6, and 8 weeks post starting treatment. Dogs will also undergo weekly physical examinations for any physical changes while on study. The tumor will undergo a biopsy before treatment, at day 14, and surgical resection will be considered at the end of study.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks: Risks of anesthesia, risk of pain/discomfort, irritation, or wound at the tumor site after treatment. Risk of antibody development and subsequent anaphylactic response to vaccine

d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria: At least one measurable cutaneous or subcutaneous tumor of the following types: mast cell tumor, melanoma (also will accept oral melanoma), soft tissue sarcoma, and thyroid tumors. No concurrent chemotherapy or immunotherapy.

d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name: Cowpea mosaic virus (CPMV)  non-enveloped plant virus of the comovirus group. CPMV particles evoke strong antitumor immunity by activating both innate and adaptive immune responses across various murine tumor models. CPMV stimulates a potent antitumor immune response in mouse models of melanoma, ovarian cancer, breast cancer, colon cancer and glioma. CPMV does not replicate in mammals and can be administered in high doses with minimal toxicity. CPMV and its RNA-free counterpart, “empty (e) CPMV”, are highly immunogenic, efficiently produced in plants, scalable to produce, and chemically modifiable. CPMV injected directly into an identified primary tumor relieve immunosuppression by inducing fast recruitment of antigen presenting cells (APCs) in tumors. Innate cells in tumors tend to be immunosuppressive and have poor antigen-presenting capabilities; CPMV treatment changes the tumor microenvironment (TME) to immunostimulatory, i.e., reprogramming M2 macrophages to M1 macrophages and infiltrating N1 neutrophils. These innate immune cells have activated receptors [TLRs; specifically, CPMV activates TLR2, 4, and 7] and mature, process antigens within the tumor, and express CD80, CD86, and MHC Class II. The innate cells then travel to the draining lymph nodes, where they effectively present the tumor-associated antigens. This cascade of events leads to adaptive responses, including increased tumor infiltration by tumor antigen-specific CD4+ and CD8+ effector T cells and memory T cells.

d_sv_content.name: Clinical trial for dogs newly diagnosed with osteosarcoma
d_sv_content.tagline: CLINCIAL TRIAL FOR DOGS WITH NEWLY DIAGNOSED OSTEOSARCOMA
d_sv_content.description:
In this study we will investigate the therapeutic potential of immune cells known as invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells, made from the blood of a healthy donor dog, in dogs with bone cancer. iNKT cells are potent immune cells that have been shown to kill cancer cells in mouse models and in some human cancer patients. The iNKT cells directly kill the tumor (cancer cell) and  they also boost the patient's own anti-tumor (cancer-killing) immune responses. In this study, we will genetically modify these natural killer T cells (NKT) cells to express a protein known as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR). The CAR directs the genetically modified CAR-iNKT cells to a target protein (known as B7H3) on the bone cancer cell. The CAR-iNKT cells kill the bone cancer cells and activate the immune system to do the same. The purpose of this study is to determine i) the safety of CAR-iNKT cells, ii) their ability to traffic to the bone tumor in your dog’s leg and exert an anti-cancer effect there, iii) their ability to delay or prevent metastatic disease and iv) how long the CAR-iNKT cells remain in your dog’s body. 


This clinical trial is fully funded and at no cost to owners. Covered procedures include:

  1. Bloodwork for general health screening
  2. Chest radiographs to be sure the osteosarcoma has not spread to the lungs prior to treatment
  3. Bone biopsy to confirm osteosarcoma and the presence of the B7H3 target protein
  4. Cellular therapy with iNKT cells
  5. Amputation of the affected limb (~10 days after cell therapy) and all post-op care/hospitalization
  6. Standard of care chemotherapy
  7. Follow up monitoring of bloodwork and chest radiographs


All clinical trial visits are in person at the University of Pennsylvania School of Veterinary Medicine in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: Your dog’s osteosarcoma may get better, stay the same, or get worse while participating in this study. We may learn additional information about your dog’s disease that may affect how your dog is treated, and your dog’s participation in this study may help other pets with the same disease in the future.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks: Possible risks include but are not limited to reduced white blood cell count, infection, fever, allergic reactions, low blood pressure, weakness, and shock.

1. Dogs newly diagnosed with osteosarcoma who's owners would like to pursue amputation
  2. Adequate heart, liver and kidney function
  3. Weight of at least 50l,bs (23kg)
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
1. Osteosarcoma that has already metastasized
  2. Other severe concurrent disease

d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_endpoint: Your dog will be in the study until his or her osteosarcoma progresses, or for up to 18 months. Up to a total of 25 dogs will be enrolled in this study. d_sv_content.name: Feasibility and dose-optimization clinical trial of local immunotherapy for solid tumors in canine cancer patients
d_sv_content.tagline: Intra-tumoral T-cell Engager Therapy for Canine Soft Tissue Sarcoma
d_sv_content.description:
WHY IS THIS STUDY BEING DONE?

Immunotherapies are a class of anti-cancer treatments that work by activating a patient’s own immune system to fight specific diseases, including cancer. A number of immunotherapies have been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in humans in a wide range of diseases, including cancer. While these therapies have shown positive results in cancers of blood cells, they have had more limited successes in solid tumors like soft tissue sarcoma. This is thought to be in part because it is hard to get enough of the drug into the tumor when it is given through the blood stream (intravenously) without causing serious side effects. To overcome this limitation, this research study will use injections of immunotherapies directly through the skin into the tumor (intra-tumoral injections). 


The primary goal of this research study is to test whether it is safe and feasible to treat tumors by injecting them with a certain type of immunotherapy called T-cell engagers (TCEs).  A T cell is a special kind of white blood cell that attacks sick cells in your body, including virus-infected cells and cancer cells. TCEs are a new kind of cancer immunotherapy that helps a patient’s own T cells find and kill cancer cells. They work like a connector: one end sticks to a cancer cell, and the other end sticks to a T cell. By pulling the two cells together, the TCE helps the T cell recognize the cancer cell and activate its killing response. In this research study, two different TCEs will be tested together (TCE combination). They work in much the same way, but each one attaches to different markers on cancer cells and T cells. Because they target different markers, the two treatments can help T cells kill cancer cells more effectively, even at lower doses of each TCE, which helps reduce the chance of harmful side effects. The goal is to make the therapy work better while still keeping patients safe.


The study will test different doses of TCEs per injection, different numbers of injections placed into the tumor itself, and the product used to dilute the TCEs. The TCE combination will be diluted either in sterile saline (a solution of salt and water) or in hydrogel (a water-based gel). The hydrogel’s job is to slowly release the drugs into the tumor, with the goal to keep the cancer cells exposed to the drugs for a longer time. This may help the treatment work better and could also reduce side effects. The TCE combination will also be mixed with sterile fluorescent dye(s) that will help researchers track where the injections were placed in the tumor. The fluorescent dye(s) have already been used in multiple canine and human clinical trials with no known side effects.  


The “investigational” part of the study are the intratumoral injections of the TCE combinations diluted in sterile saline or hydrogel. These TCEs are investigational drugs, which means they have not yet been approved by the FDA or the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) for use in dogs or other species. The purpose of this study is to test the safety and the biological effect of the TCE combination in canine patients with soft tissue sarcoma (STS), rather than to specifically provide medical treatment to the enrolled patient.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: It is not currently known whether dogs enrolled in this study will benefit from intra-tumoral treatment with these TCEs at these doses or at any dose. This is one of the questions the study sponsor is interested in answering through this study. A benefit may come as an anti-tumor response, a reduced risk of tumor recurrence or spread after removal, and/or an improvement in quality of life and survival should the treatment result in an anti-tumor response or lowered risk of spread or recurrence. It is possible that the study drug will have no clinical benefit. It is also possible that a patient enrolled in this study may experience negative side effects from the drug.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks:
WHAT ARE THE RISKS OF THE STUDY?


Risks to patient: 


The standard laboratory tests (blood work), ultrasound, sedation, anesthesia, and surgery carry the same risks they would if the patient were undergoing these procedures outside of the study. The TCEs under investigation have the potential to cause unwanted side effects. These unwanted side effects, anticipated to the best of our current knowledge based on studies in dogs with various tumor types, are also described below.


Blood sample collection: A small needle will be inserted into the vein of the enrolled patient to take blood samples. The total amount of blood to be obtained for study related procedures at any given visit is typically less that 5ml (roughly 1 teaspoon). Risks associated with blood draw may include some discomfort, mild irritation at the collection site, bruising, and rarely infection. Blood draws are part of standard of care for anesthesia and cancer treatment in general and may be done whether the patient participates in this study or not. The addition of intratumorally injected TCEs is not expected to alter the safety of blood sample collection. 


Tumor ultrasound: There are no known risks associated with performing ultrasound other than possible mild discomfort from pressure placed on the ultrasound probe throughout the examination. 


Surgery: The surgical protocol will be performed according to standard of care, which means that there is nothing experimental about the surgery portion of the study. There is currently no evidence to indicate that any of these standard surgical and anesthesia risks will be increased by the study drug evaluated in this study. The surgeon can discuss any standard surgery risks, including bleeding after surgery, infection at the surgery site, poor wound healing, and death.


Sedation/Anesthesia: Risks of sedation and anesthesia include low blood pressure, abnormal heart rhythms, bad reactions to the anesthesia drugs, and rarely, respiratory and/or cardiac arrest and death.


Immunotherapy Injections: The immunotherapy injections will occur through small needles, similar to those used for standard vaccines. Predictable risks associated with these TCE injections include temporary pain, minor bleeding from the injection sites, redness, and irritation at the injection site, particularly if the immune system responds to the injected agents. These TCEs are expected to affect the immune system. Therefore, temporary changes in the numbers of different immune cells within the tumor are anticipated. However, these changes are not expected to require treatment. At the veterinarian’s discretion, pain medication may be given before the tumor injections to reduce any discomfort. This is optional because the injections may not be any more painful than routine shots, blood draws, or other procedures that usually don’t require pain relief.


Human patients in clinical trials of other TCEs - given at higher doses into the bloodstream rather than directly into tumors - have sometimes experienced flu‑like symptoms, low blood pressure, and other side effects. In a prior canine clinical study testing intratumoral injection of a different TCE (not being used in this study), one patient experienced liver enzyme elevations and a systemic inflammatory response that resolved within a few days. Clinical signs included abdominal pain, two episodes of vomiting, dull mentation, increased heart rate, low blood pressure, and pale mucous membranes. Although this study seeks to reduce these risks through careful selection of the TCEs and the intratumoral doses to be used, these and other side effects, such as irritation at the injection site, release of release of chemicals in the body that can cause an overactive immune response, or injury to the intestines, hormonal system, heart, brain, lungs, and/or skin could occur. To reduce the risks of side effects in treated patients, all patients will be given oral diphenhydramine (Benadryl) 1-2 hours before injection (to help lower the risk of whole‑body allergic or anaphylactic reactions), patients will be monitored closely overnight following administration of the TCE, and the dose will be adjusted carefully between dose cohorts.


The dose and treatment schedule utilized in this study were selected to minimize risk experienced by each patient enrolled on this study. There also may be other side effects or risks that we cannot predict. Many side effects go away shortly after the drug treatment, but in some cases side effects can be serious or long-lasting or permanent.


During the course of this study, we may find out more information about the study drug, its safety, or efficacy that could be important. This information, once learned, will be made available.
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

  1. Informed owner consent for trial participation.
  2. At least one measurable superficial presumed soft tissue sarcoma (STS) lesion (primary or recurrent tumor) that is accessible for percutaneous injection and for which there is a planned surgical intervention. 
  3. Tumor mass must be at least three times the volume to be injected (i.e. 900 mm3 in volume if 3x100 ml of TCE in saline or hydrogel will be injected) and must have a depth of at least 1.7 cm to accommodate needle length (1.25 cm) and minimum surgical pathology margin (0.4 cm).
  4. No medical contraindication to sedation, general anesthesia, or surgery.
  5. Life expectancy > 8 weeks.

Favorable performance status based on modified Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) criteria Grade 0 or 1
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
Exclusion Criteria:

  1. Weight less than 5 kg.
  2. Tumors that are anticipated by the Investigator to lack a sufficient volume of viable tumor tissue for injection due to tumor size, location, or other features based on any available pre-operative imaging (CT or ultrasound) or pathology reports describing extensive necrosis, cystic areas, or other non-viable tumor tissue.
  3. Tumors near or involving critical structures for which, in the opinion of the treating clinician, injection would pose undue risk to the patient. 
  4. Significant co-morbidities that could, in the opinion of the Investigator, interfere with adherence to the study’s procedures or requirements, or otherwise compromise the study’s objectives.
  5. History of immune-mediated disease (immune-mediated polyarthritis [IMPA], immune-mediated hemolytic anemia [IMHA], immune-mediated thrombocytopenia [ITP], myasthenia gravis, etc.) 
  6. Creatinine > 1.5x upper limit of normal (ULN)
  7. Bilirubin > 2x ULN 
  8. Hematocrit or packed cell volume < 25%
  9. Platelets < 100,000 cells/ul
  10. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) > 2.5x ULN
  11. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) ≥ 5x ULN
  12. Use of anti-coagulants ≤ 2 weeks prior to injection.
  13. Use of any nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) ≤ 3 days prior to injection.
  14. Use of JAK inhibitors (e.g., Apoquel, Zenrelia, Numelvi) ≤ 14 days prior to injection.
  15. Use of cyclosporine ≤ 30 days prior to injection.
  16. Use of corticosteroids ≤ 7 days prior to injection.
  17. Use of immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g. Gilvetmab) ≤ 3 months prior to injection
  18. Use of other T-cell targeting agents (CAR-T Cells, monoclonal antibodies (OX40, 4-1BB, etc.) ≤ 3 months prior to injection.
d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name: Multiple different T-cell engagers (TCE) will be delivered by injection intra-tumor with either sterile saline or hydrogel. The TCEs are engineered antibodies that bind to two targets, one on a tumor cell (B7-H3 or PD-L1) and one on a T-cell (CD3 or CD28).

d_sv_content.name: Novel Immunotherapy for Cats with Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
d_sv_content.tagline: New Treatment for Cats with Oral Tumors
d_sv_content.description:
Oral squamous cell carcinoma is a very difficult cancer to treat in cats and is often fairly advanced before it is detected. This clinical trial will be examining the effectiveness of a new type of immunotherapy for treating this disease in cats, which is based on very promising data from two squamous cell carcinoma trials conducted recently in horses at CSU. This new treatment is designed to stimulate the body’s own immune defenses to attack the tumor cells and cause tumor regression or elimination. In this particular trial, even stopping the tumor from growing (rather than full elimination) would be considered a success. This immunotherapy drug has been tested previously in cats, and is generally well-tolerated, with few side-effects, but it has only been evaluated in one cat with oral squamous cell carcinoma previously. The treatment has however been extensively evaluated in horses with squamous cell carcinoma, with a high degree of success. In this study, we will evaluate this novel immunotherapy in cats with oral SCC to determine how well the treatment works and how well it is tolerated by cats.


Cats will receive four injections of the LTN immunotherapy into their tumor, which are given once every three weeks. Cats must be put under anesthesia for these injections. While under anesthesia, cats will have CT scans and tumor biopsies performed prior to starting treatment, at the time of the third injection, and 3 weeks after the 4th injection (CT only). Blood tests (complete blood count and chemistry profile) will also be performed at these visits. Study participation is completed after the visit that is 3 weeks after the last injection. A total of 5 visits and anesthetic episodes are required for this study.

d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits: Tumor shrinkage
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks: Potential side-effects of the immunotherapy include slight swelling and redness at the injection sites. Other side-effects may include lethargy and partial inappetence that may last for 24 hours or slightly longer. Potential side-effects of general anesthesia include changes in kidney function or heart function. To help avoid these, my cat will receive fluid therapy and will be closely monitored by an experienced staff. In very rare cases, anesthesia may result in stoppage of the heart and/or breathing.
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
1. Cats with a confirmed diagnosis of oral squamous cell carcinoma of the gums, tongue, lips, or bony tissues of the jaw with tumor accessible for injections
  2. No tumor spread beyond local lymph nodes
  3. Good function of liver and kidneys and free of severe underlying disease
  4. Cats must be healthy enough to undergo multiple anesthetic events
  5. Pets must come to CSU for all visits related to the clinical trial
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
1. Tumors on the ear or nose
  2. Spread beyond local lymph nodes
  3. Any significant concurrent conditions, including advanced chronic kidney disease, active liver disease, or diabetes mellitus
  4. Currently receiving immune suppressive medications

d_sv_content.name: Near-Infrared Fluorescence Imaging with Indocyanine Green for Intraoperative Detection of Canine Urothelial Carcinoma
d_sv_content.tagline: Using a Fluorescent Dye to Identify Bladder Tumors in Dogs During Surgery
d_sv_content.description: Urothelial carcinoma (UC) is the most common type of bladder cancer in dogs. For dogs with tumors in certain locations, surgical removal (partial cystectomy) can improve outcomes with low risk. New minimally invasive techniques that maintain a closed bladder may offer additional benefits and warrant further investigation, but these approaches currently rely on specialized camera equipment within the bladder, which is not always available, to identify tumors. This pilot study will test whether a safe dye, indocyanine green (ICG), used with near-infrared (NIR) imaging can identify bladder tumors and their edges during surgery. The findings with NIR will be compared with what is seen by the surgeon and with microscopic examination by a pathologist. Results will be incorporated into future studies with novel surgical techniques that have the potential to improve outcomes in dogs with UC.
d_sv_content.requirements: Dogs enrolled in the study will receive a single intravenous injection of ICG approximately 24 hours before their planned surgery for bladder tumor removal, and a special near-infrared camera will be used during the procedure to assess whether the tumor and its margins fluoresce differently than surrounding normal tissue. ICG is an FDA-approved dye that is commonly used for other imaging purposes in human and veterinary medicine, but its use for identifying bladder tumors during surgery in dogs is considered investigational and its effectiveness for this purpose has not yet been established. A total of five dogs will be enrolled in this study, and all dogs will receive the same dye injection and imaging procedure during their planned surgery; there are no separate treatment or control groups. Study participation is complete after surgery is performed.
d_sv_content.responsibilities: You are responsible for the initial exam fee, costs to confirm the diagnosis of UC, the cost of the bladder tumor removal beyond the credit that is provided by the study, and hospitalization after surgery, and any other tests recommended by your pet’s oncologist. You are also responsible for the costs of treatment in the case of any adverse events unrelated to the study. You are expected to make and keep all appointments, according to the clinical trial protocol.
d_sv_content.whoCan: Dogs must have a confirmed diagnosis of urothelial carcinoma (either by tumor sampling (cytology or biopsy) or positive BRAF mutational testing) that is considered amenable to surgery (partial cystectomy). They cannot have received any prior treatment for their tumor other than non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications. They must be healthy enough to undergo general anesthesia and receive the contrast agent (ICG) and cannot have evidence of spread of their tumor beyond the bladder.
d_sv_content.benefits: Possible benefits include that the extent of your dog's cancer may be better visualized during surgery. The risks associated with this study are largely those associated with the standard of care for dogs undergoing routine diagnostic tests, anesthesia, and surgery for removal of bladder tumors. These risks will be discussed in detail prior to study enrollment.
d_sv_content.compensation: Once dogs are enrolled in the study, the study will pay the following costs: all costs surrounding the ICG imaging agent including its administration and near-infrared camera use for its detection in tissues during surgery. In addition, the study will provide a credit of $2,690 to your account at the VTH to be put towards the cost of the bladder surgery visit as a benefit of enrollment in this trial.
d_sv_content.timeCommitment: The study requires two visits: one the day before surgery and then the following day for surgery to remove the tumor. The visit the day before surgery will need to happen in the morning and will likely take 2-3 hours. On the day of surgery, your dog will be in the hospital all day and stay in hospital overnight for monitoring.

d_sv_content.description:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a fast-growing cancer of the blood and bone marrow that affects both people and dogs. Dogs diagnosed with AML usually have a poor outlook, and current treatments only extend survival for a short time, typically about 1–2 months.

Researchers are looking for better treatment options for dogs with AML. Many dogs with AML have changes (mutations) in a gene called NRAS, which can cause cancer cells to grow and survive. This study is testing a medication called trametinib, which blocks signals that cancer cells use to grow.

This trial is being led by the Clinical Hematopathology Laboratory in partnership with the Flint Animal Cancer Center of the Colorado State University Veterinary Health System and is sponsored by the Lutsen Linder Research Fund for Extremely Gorgeous Dogs.

d_sv_content.description:
This study is evaluating a new limb-sparing surgery for dogs with bone cancer (osteosarcoma). Instead of removing the limb, this approach uses a custom 3D-printed implant to replace the diseased bone.

The implant is designed specifically for your dog using advanced imaging and is made from a material that can gradually be replaced by your dog’s own bone over time. The goal is to maintain limb function while treating the cancer.

Dogs in this study will undergo surgery followed by chemotherapy and long-term monitoring to evaluate how well the implant works and how the cancer responds to treatment.

d_sv_content.name: Minimally invasive sentinel lymph node mapping for dogs with anal sac adenocarcinoma (AGASACA)
d_sv_content.tagline: Finding draining lymph nodes for anal gland tumors in dogs using minimally invasive surgery
d_sv_content.description: Local lymph nodes are a common site for the cancer to spread in dogs with anal sac tumors. A safe and common test to find the lymph nodes that drain fluid from a tumor is sentinel lymph node (SLN) mapping. However, the lymph nodes that drain anal sac tumors are located within the abdomen and pelvis, which means that SLN mapping in dogs with anal sac tumors has needed open abdominal surgery. Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) has many reported benefits for patients compared to open abdominal surgery, including smaller incisions, reduced pain, and earlier return to function. The goal of this study is to evaluate SLN mapping techniques via a MIS approach in dogs with anal sac tumors and compare the results to other methods.
d_sv_content.requirements: There are two visits required for this study. At the first visit, dogs will undergo general anesthesia for CT scan of the abdomen and intra-pelvic region. An injection of a contrast agent will be given locally near the tumor with subsequent CT imaging to identify the first lymph node(s) that drain the tumor (SLN). This is a routine pre-surgical imaging technique used to further characterize the regional lymph nodes prior to surgery and has previously been shown to be effective. The second visit will occur within 7 days of the first visit. At this visit, dogs will be anesthetized for standard of care surgery with removal of the anal sac tumor and concurrent intraoperative lymph node mapping via a MIS approach and removal of regional lymph nodes within the abdomen or pelvic canal that are of concern/at risk for harboring cancer cells. All removed tissue samples will be submitted for biopsy to determine tumor type and evidence of cancer cells within the lymph nodes. The study is complete after the second visit.

d_sv_content.tagline: COTC033: Help us test a new approach to treat cancer by using vaccine immunity in dogs.
d_sv_content.description:
This study is for dogs that have cancer. Veterinarians and researchers want to see if common vaccines can be repurposed to help a dog’s immune system fight cancer. d_sv_content.description:

CAR T cell therapy uses your dog’s own immune cells to help fight cancer. A blood sample is collected (about 3-4 tablespoons), and special immune cells (called T cells) are modified in a lab to better recognize and attack cancer cells. Dogs in this study will also receive medications to prepare the body for treatment and to support the immune system during the study. The goal is to determine if this treatment is safe and effective for dogs with metastatic bone cancer.

d_sv_content.tagline: A research study evaluating a novel drug alongside radiation therapy for dogs with brain tumors.
d_sv_content.description:
Dogs diagnosed with glioma, an aggressive brain tumor, often experience limited benefit from standard treatments such as radiation therapy alone. This clinical trial is evaluating a novel investigational drug called bisaminoquinoline-13 (BAQ-13) that may help improve how brain tumors respond to radiation therapy.

d_sv_content.name: Assessing a new technique to shrink liver tumors in dogs
d_sv_content.tagline: Help us learn more about this new technique that could shrink liver tumors in dogs!
d_sv_content.description:
When liver tumors in dogs cannot be removed with surgery, treatment options are limited or non-existent. In humans, one of the standard treatments for those cases is transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), which eliminates the blood supply of the tumor and may decrease tumor size. d_sv_content.tagline: Help us study a new technique to place urethral stents in dogs with prostate, bladder, and/or urethra tumors!
d_sv_content.description:
Cancer resulting in obstruction of the lower urinary tract of dogs is most commonly found in the prostate, urinary bladder and urethra (tube responsible for draining urine out of the body). Unfortunately, cancer of the lower urinary tract often results in complete blockage of the urethra, causing a patient to be unable to pass urine. The inability to urinate is a life-threatening emergency.

The placement of urethral stents is generally performed with fluoroscopic-guidance (use of “real-time” x-rays). While fluoroscopy is useful for stent placement, there may be other techniques that could be considered. Traditionally, ultrasonographic assessment of tumor size and location has been performed by transabdominal ultrasound (where the ultrasound probe is placed on the abdominal wall to allow for visualization of organs within the abdomen), but this method can be inaccurate. The use of transrectal ultrasound (where an ultrasound probe is placed into the rectum) circumvents these previously discussed problems, and therefore, the purpose of this study is to evaluate this technique for efficacy.

d_sv_content.name: Comparing laser removal with and without photodynamic therapy for the treatment of ear sarcoids in horses
d_sv_content.tagline: Ear sarcoid treatment in horses
d_sv_content.description:
The purpose of this study is to compare the treatment of ear sarcoids in horses to see if the addition of photodynamic therapy (PDT) provides a lower rate of recurrence and faster healing time compared to regular laser excision. Sarcoids are the most common type of cancer identified in horses.


Tumors may be quiescent for a period of time, but most eventually become aggressive and highly invasive, extending into surrounding tissues and causing significant discomfort. Several treatment methods have been used to treat sarcoids, including surgical removal, cryotherapy, laser therapy, topical and local injectable chemotherapies, electrochemotherapy, and immunotherapy. When managing sarcoids on the ear, recurrence remains a concern, as wide tissue margins are necessary to ensure optimal outcomes. Obtaining large surgical margins in the inner and outer ears can be challenging due to the ear's contour. 


Combining photodynamic therapy (PDT) with diode laser excision may offer enhanced disease control. PDT uses light of a specific wavelength to target a dye that has been applied to the cancerous tissues and kills the cancer cells after activation with the laser. It is anticipated that the addition of PDT to diode laser tumor removal will provide better disease control (lower recurrence) and improve surgical wound healing. Sarcoid treatment that offers improved disease control and faster wound healing would be beneficial in areas that are often difficult to treat, such as the ear. If the use of PDT improves outcomes in this subset of horses, the treatment could be applied to select sarcoids in other anatomic locations.
d_sv_content.requirements: If the exams and tests show that your horse can take part in the study, and you choose to enroll them, then the following will happen as part of the study:The horse will be randomly assigned to Group 1 or Group 2 for treatment purposes.Horses in Group 1 will be sedated or undergo general anesthesia for laser removal of the sarcoid of the ear. This is the standard of care for the treatment of ear sarcoids.Horses in Group 2 will undergo the same laser excision procedure as in Group 1 (receiving the standard of care for the treatment of ear sarcoids) and will also undergo photodynamic therapy (PDT) immediately following the laser removal. For PDT, a green dye (infracyanine green) will be applied to the surgical site and then treated with a different type of laser.
d_sv_content.responsibilities: If you wish to have your horse participate in this study, you will be responsible for daily monitoring of the surgical site for the first 3 weeks, keeping it clean and protected from flies. You will be asked to photograph the surgical site every 2-3 days and to share the photographs with the research team until the first recheck. An initial recheck recommendation will be made three weeks following surgery to evaluate wound healing and for any signs of sarcoid recurrence. Additional recheck appointments will be scheduled at 3, 6, and 12 months postoperatively, or sooner if you or your primary veterinarian observes suspected regrowth. You will be requested to photograph the surgical site once per month and submit the photographs to the investigators.
d_sv_content.whoCan: Before your horse begins the study, your horse will need to have the following examination to find out if he/she can be in the study:Full physical examinationExamination of the affected ear(s) by a board-certified equine surgeon and/or internal medicine specialist to determine if the sarcoid is appropriate for surgical intervention.Horses will be excluded if the entire ear is effaced by the tumor or if there is clear cartilage involvement
d_sv_content.benefits: We cannot guarantee any benefits to your horse or other animals from your participation in this clinical trial; however, potential benefits may include improved disease control (reduced recurrence) and improved surgical wound healing. This would be a direct medical benefit to your horse. You will also receive histopathologic confirmation (tissue evaluated by a pathologist) of the tumor type as part of this study, regardless of treatment group. Additionally, the information from this study may guide future treatment of skin cancers in horses. Adverse effects/risks of sedation/anesthesia include (but are not limited to) lethargy following procedure, anaphylactic reactions to medications, cardiovascular collapse, respiratory depression, minor or major orthopedic injury, increased risk of colic, and/or aspiration pneumonia, up to and including death. Oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medication (flunixin meglumine) can cause acute kidney injury or worsen pre-existing kidney disease. Risks associated with the surgical site include excessive hemorrhage and/or infection that may require additional therapy. Regrowth of the sarcoid is possible and will be monitored throughout the study period (1-year duration). At the time regrowth is noted, you may then elect to pursue additional/repeated treatment (not covered by this study).

d_sv_content.name: Treatment of Canine Sarcoma with FAP CAR T-cells (FAP CAR-T Study)
d_sv_content.tagline: New treatment with autologous FAP CAR T-cells for sarcomas
d_sv_content.description:
CAR T cell therapy has fundamentally changed how certain cancers are treated. By reprogramming a patient's own T lymphocytes to express a receptor targeting a protein on tumor cells, it directs the immune system to destroy them, producing durable remissions in blood cancers once refractory to conventional treatment.


These benefits have yet to reach veterinary patients, and some cancers remain especially hard to treat with immunotherapy. Sarcomas can be very resistant to standard treatment across many species, including dogs. Led by investigators at Colorado State University, we are testing CAR T cells engineered against FAP, a protein highly expressed in many sarcomas, in pet dogs. We are evaluating both the therapy's activity and its side effects. Advancing this work meets a real clinical need for companion animals while accelerating progress for human patients as well.


In this study, we will test a new treatment for dogs with sarcomas. As the tumor has to be biopsied, this study is best for sarcomas that are external or on the outside of the body.
d_sv_content.requirements: This new treatment uses special cells called CAR T cells, prepared as follows:We take immune cells (T cells) that fight disease in your dog's body with a blood drawWe change these cells in a lab so they can find and attack cells that support the tumor's growthWe give your dog oral chemotherapy (Cytoxan) over two days to reduce their natural population of immune cellsWe give these improved cells back to your dog through an infusion directly into the blood stream.The changed T cells are released into the body and will search and kill special cells that help tumors grow called fibroblasts. By attacking these support cells, the treatment aims to damage the tumor's ability to grow and spread and help fight the cancer.
d_sv_content.responsibilities: If your pet joins the study, you must:Pay for tests to see if your pet can joinBring your pet to all appointments (8 required visits over approximately 2.5 months)Consent to a tumor biopsy prior to CAR T cell infusionBring your pet for surgery or, if you do not wish to pursue surgery, a second biopsy 2 weeks after CAR T cells infusionIf your pet dies for any reason, we ask permission to do an autopsy to learn more. We need blood samples at different times during the study. Any samples we collect become property of UC Davis.
d_sv_content.whoCan: Your pet must be at least 1 year old, weigh at least 11 kg, and have:A sarcoma on the outside of the body that can be biopsiedOther inclusion and exclusion criteria can be talked about in more detail with the research team.
d_sv_content.benefits: BenefitsWe cannot promise that your pet will benefit from this study. We are still learning if this treatment works. However, possible benefits include:The tumor might get smaller or respond to treatmentYour pet's symptoms might improveYour pet might live longerRisksThis treatment is experimental. The FDA has not approved it. We cannot promise it will work or be safe.Risks from the tumor biopsy: These risks are uncommon but may include:pain or discomfort at the biopsy site (common, usually mild and managed with pain medication)Infection at the biopsy site (uncommon)Bleeding or bruising (uncommon)Broken bone at the biopsy site for bone tumors (rare)Complications from sedation or anesthesia, including allergic reaction or, very rarely, death (rare, estimated <1% in healthy dogs)Risks from chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide) given prior to CAR T-cell therapy:Upset stomach, vomiting, or decreased appetite (common, usually mild and self-limiting)Low blood cell counts, which could increase risk of bleeding or infection (common but expected to be mild)Sterile hemorrhagic cystitis (bladder irritation causing bloody urine) (uncommon)Severe infection due to low white blood cell counts, which may need hospitalization and can rarely result in deathRisks from CAR T-cell infusion: Please note: CAR T-cell therapy has been studied in dogs, but CAR T-cells targeting FAP specifically have not been extensively tested. Five dogs have been enrolled so far at other vet schools (Colorado State University and Tufts Vet School) and tolerated the treatment without significant side effects. Because this is a new treatment, there may be unknown risks.Fever (common in human patients, expected to be manageable)Cytokine release syndrome (CRS): an inflammatory response that can cause fever, low blood pressure, and difficulty breathing. In humans, CRS ranges from mild (common) to severe (uncommon). Severe CRS can be life-threatening but is treatable if caught early.Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS): neurological symptoms such as confusion, tremors, or seizures (rare in humans, unknown frequency in dogs)"On-target, off-tumor" effects: the CAR T-cells might attack healthy tissues that express FAP (unknown risk)Secondary malignancy: very rarely, CAR T-cells themselves could become cancerous (very rare, reported in humans)Infusion reactions such as hives, itching, or vomiting (uncommon, usually mild)How complications will be addressed:All study-related side effects will be treated by the veterinary team at UC Davis Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital. Your dog will be closely monitored throughout the study, including hourly monitoring on the day of CAR T-cell infusion. If any problems arise, the study team will provide prompt medical care. However, as with any experimental treatment, some problems could be serious enough to cause death.The study will pay up to $2,500 for treatment of study-related side effects. This coverage applies only to treatment at UC Davis. Costs exceeding $2,500, or treatment obtained elsewhere, are the owner's responsibility.

d_sv_content.description:
Nasal tumors can cause severe nasal bleeding or discharge and difficulty breathing. These tumors often aggressively spread throughout the tissues of the nasal cavity and into the surrounding organs, including the eye and brain. Radiation therapy is the treatment of choice for nasal tumors in dogs; however, radiation therapy isn't often good for long-term control of the tumor. An another treatment option is transarterial embolization, or TAE, which involves the delivery of a mechanical “clot” to the main arteries supplying blood to the tissues of the nasal cavity with the goal of eliminating the blood supply of the tumor and decreasing tumor size.

The purposes of this study are to 1) describe TAE in dogs with naturally-occurring nasal cancer, 2) evaluate the effect that nasal TAE has on the tumor, and 3) evaluate the effect that nasal TAE has on the values measured by positron emission tomography (PET) scanning.

d_sv_content.description:
Canine Cutaneous Epitheliotropic T-cell Lymphoma (CETCL) is a rare but aggressive skin cancer in dogs, and sadly, most affected dogs live less than a year after diagnosis, even with chemotherapy. One major reason for this poor prognosis is that we don’t fully understand how the disease develops or progresses, which has made it difficult to create new, effective treatments.

This study aims to change that. By analyzing the microRNA (miRNA) in the skin of dogs with CETCL, we hope to uncover key markers that could help diagnose the disease earlier, predict how it will progress, and track treatment effectiveness. Research in humans with similar cancers has shown that identifying these miRNAs could also lead to the development of new treatment options. Ultimately, our goal is to improve the way we diagnose and care for dogs with CETCL, giving them a better chance for a longer, healthier life.
d_sv_content.requirements:
If you choose to enroll your dog in this study, the team at the UC Davis Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital will collect up to four small skin samples (each about 8mm) from affected areas of your dog’s skin. These areas might include patches, plaques, tumors, or spots with discoloration or crusting, depending on your dog’s condition. Before taking these skin samples, the veterinary team will also collect surface samples from the lesions to check for any bacterial infections.
By participating, you'll be helping us advance research to better understand this type of skin cancer and develop more effective treatments for dogs.
d_sv_content.responsibilities: You will be responsible for submitting all records related to your dog’s diagnosis. Once we determine eligibility, you will need to bring your dog to the UC Davis Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital (VMTH) for the skin biopsy.
d_sv_content.whoCan: You will be asked to bring your dog into the VMTH during the work week for a short bipsy appointment.
d_sv_content.benefits:
Benefits:
There may be no direct benefit to your animal from his/her participation in this study. However, such participation may lead to discoveries about your animal’s skin disease and, therefore, may influence the course of treatment of other animals in the future.
Risks:
The administration of local anesthesia (i.e., local “freezing”) and collecting skin biopsies may also cause minor and momentary discomfort, too. If skin biopsies are collected from your animal, there is also a risk that the biopsy sites may become infected within the 10–14-day post-operative period. However, the risk of infection at the skin biopsy sites is relatively low with appropriate post-operative care. Clinical signs that would indicate the presence of a bacterial infection at the biopsy sites would include redness, swelling, heat, pain, malodor, and/or discharge. If your animal develops a skin infection within 10-14 days of biopsy collection as a direct result of the procedure, the study veterinarian will pay for appropriate treatment at the UC Davis Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital, which may include oral and/or topical antimicrobials, until resolution. Beyond this, you will be responsible for the cost of continued care in consultation with your veterinarian. If skin biopsies are collected from your animal, the skin may also heal by forming a small scar which may not regrow hair.

d_sv_content.name: Hypophysectomy for cats with Pituitary Tumors
d_sv_content.tagline: Profiling the immune-endocrine interface in feline hypersomatotropism through hypophysectomy
d_sv_content.description:
Feline hypersomatotropism is an endocrine disorder caused by excessive secretion of growth hormone from a pituitary tumor. This disease can lead to difficult control of diabetes, progressive organ enlargement, cardiac and renal dysfunction, and compression on of the brain by the growing tumor, ultimately causing life-threatening decompensation. To date, the surgical removal of the pituitary tumor, hypophysectomy, is the only treatment that can definitively restore normal hormone levels. 


This study explores how the immune system interacts with pituitary tumors in cats. After removal of the pituitary tumor, we will study the tumor composition and gene activity. We will also explore how immune responses relate to hormone levels, helping us better understand the link between the immune system and hormonal health. Understanding this relationship could help explain how these tumors behave and reveal promising directions for future treatment.
d_sv_content.requirements: Cats should have an IGF-1 blood test with their veterinarian to help determine whether they qualify for the study. UC Davis veterinarians will then assess whether your cat is a good candidate for hypophysectomy. Participation includes surgery to remove the pituitary tumor as well as two follow-up visits.​The trial will consist of the following phases:​​Screening​Enrollment​SurgeryRechecks (2)
d_sv_content.responsibilities: While the cost of the surgery (hypophysectomy) is covered by the study, the rest of the cost of care fees such hospitalization, medications, diagnostic tests (bloodwork, radiograph, ultrasound, continuous glucose monitor), remains the responsibility of the owner. We will ask you to bring your cat to the UC Davis Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital 1 and 3 weeks after the procedure for a recheck.
d_sv_content.whoCan: Cats that were determined by a UC Davis VMTH veterinarian to be a good study participant for this study are eligible to enroll. Cats must be between the ages of 1 and 15 at the time of enrollment.
d_sv_content.benefits: Benefits​​For cats participating in this study, removal of the pituitary tumor may allow improvement of the clinical signs and remission of the diabetes, if present. Financial support helps cover the cost of surgery (hypophysectomy).​​Risks​Hypophysectomy is a surgical intervention that may results in blood loss, brain injury, infection, palate dehiscence, and dry eye. Removing the pituitary tumor may lead to rapid changes in electrolytes and glucose regulation. Cats that undergo hypophysectomy must remain on hormonal supplements. Because hypophysectomy is a critical procedure, cats can die during or after the surgery. ​
d_sv_content.compensation: The cost of the hypophysectomy procedure will be covered by the study. The study may also cover additional costs associated with surgery, anesthesia, and study-related imaging, depending on the individual patient’s needs. Owners will be responsible for costs not covered by the study, which may include hospitalization, medications, diagnostic testing, and other aspects of their pet’s clinical care. The study team will review anticipated costs and study coverage with owners prior to enrollment.
d_sv_content.timeCommitment: Approximately 31 days from enrollment through surgery and follow-up visits.

d_sv_content.name: Characterization of naturally occurring osteosarcoma in dogs
d_sv_content.tagline: Help us understand how osteosarcoma affects dogs!
d_sv_content.description:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the outcomes for dogs treated palliatively with standard amputation (no chemotherapy). Recent data indicates that at least 35% of dogs do not appear to benefit from standard chemotherapy for this disease. To better understand whether chemotherapy is truly beneficial, this trial aims to document the outcomes prospectively and accurately for dogs whose owners have elected to treat only with surgery (amputation).

There will be about 120 dogs taking part in this study across North America. Study sites include UC Davis, Purdue University, University of Wisconsin, Madison, Tufts University and Ohio State University.
d_sv_content.requirements:
Before your pet begins the study, your pet will need to have the following tests and/or procedures to find out if he/she can be in the study: bloodwork, urinalysis, chest x-rays, and abdominal ultrasound.  If a diagnosis has not been made, additional diagnostic tests such as a fine needle aspirate may be required to determine a diagnosis.  These tests are routinely performed prior to considering treatment for osteosarcoma.

If the exams, tests, and procedures show that your pet can take part in the study, and you choose to enroll them, then the following will happen as part of the study:


- Amputation of the affected limb


- Weeks 3, 9 and 15 evaluations: blood collection, (chest x-rays at week 9 and 15)


- Every 8 weeks (after week 15 visit): blood and feces collection, recheck chest x-rays, CBC


- Each of the listed visits must take place at the UC Davis Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital and are required for participation in the trial. 


- Consent for a necropsy (autopsy, if your pet dies) is required to be eligible for this study
d_sv_content.whoCan: Dogs weighing more than 25kg (55 lbs) who have been diagnosed with an osteosarcoma in the legParticipants cannot have any evidence of metastatic disease or have received prior therapy
d_sv_content.benefits: We cannot promise any benefits to your pet or other animals from your taking part in this clinical trial; however, possible benefits include reduced pain and improved quality of life and time of survival.
d_sv_content.compensation: If you continue the study until week 15, the study will pay the cost of amputation, follow-up appointments and examinations, blood tests, and x-rays after surgery. If you elect to start your dog on chemotherapy prior to week 15 (after surgery), your dog will be ineligible to continue the study and you will be responsible for costs associated with amputation.
d_sv_content.timeCommitment: Your pet will remain in the study up to 2-years or until they develop progression or spread of osteosarcoma.

d_sv_content.name: Fluorescence Imaging with PDL1-IRDye800 to Guide Surgical Treatment of Oral Cancer in Dogs
d_sv_content.tagline: New theragnostic agent (diagnostic and therapeutic) to improve our ability to effectively treat oral cancer!
d_sv_content.description:
For dogs diagnosed with oral cancer (Squamous Cell Carcinoma, Oral Malignant Melanoma), curative intent surgical removal has been consistently found to have the longest remission rate. However, conventional diagnostic imaging, which we use to plan our surgery, is imperfect and can underestimate the extent of the tumor which results in the potential that not all cancer cells are removed during surgery. This directly impacts patient outcomes (disease free interval and overall survival). There is a critical need to improve our ability to detect cancer intraoperatively (i.e. during the surgery) to improve patient outcomes.


Further, for human head and neck cancer the standard of care is to give immunotherapy (drugs that improve the immune system's ability to fight off cancer) prior to surgery, which has resulted in increased survival in a subset of patients. We have no data on this type of pre-surgical treatment in dogs, and if it would also improve patient survival times.


The purpose of this study is to evaluate the use of a theranostic agent (diagnostic and therapeutic) before surgery to improve our ability to effectively treat oral cancer. This agent is an immunotherapeutic drug (anti-PDL1) bound to a fluorophore. This drug would be given 2X before treatment (surgery or other).


Through this study we will determine if this drug can allow us to see residual cancer cells during surgery (differentiate cancer from healthy tissue) and if treatment of the tumor before surgery with the drug can improve the local anti-tumor immune response (decreased in percent viable cells in the tumor).


If successful this could overall vastly improve our ability to treat oral cancer in dogs.
d_sv_content.requirements: An initial screening and eligibility workup, including physical examination, full blood work, urinalysisA pre-operative biopsy performed at enrollment, to confirm squamous cell carcinoma or melanomaIntravenous administration of the anti-PDL1-IRDye 800 theranostic probe twice before surgeryNear infrared fluorescence Imaging performed at 8 hours, 24 hours, and 48 hours after probe deliveryRepeat biopsy or curative intent surgery after the second anti-PDL1-IRDye 800 probe administrationFollow-up visits at 7 days and 4 weeks
d_sv_content.responsibilities: If you choose to enroll your dog in this study, you will be responsible for:Covering the cost of initial screening and tests required to determine eligibility (excluding biopsy which is covered by the study)Binging your dog to all scheduled hospital visits, treatments, imaging appointments, and follow-up evaluationsCover the costs of oral tumor work up and treatment. (you will receive a $1500 incentive towards therapy). All additional hospitalization time is also covered by the study.Providing complete and accurate medical history and records as requested by the study teamMonitoring your dog at home and promptly reporting any health changes or concerns to the study teamFollowing all study-related instructions, including medication schedules and post-procedure careCommunicating with the study team if you are unable to attend a visit or if you are considering withdrawing from the studyParticipation is voluntary, and you may withdraw your dog from the study at any time.
d_sv_content.whoCan: Dogs may be eligible if they:Have a confirmed diagnosis of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) or oral malignant melanoma (OMM).Are otherwise healthy enough for anesthesia and repeated hospital visits
d_sv_content.benefits: Potential BenefitsThere is currently no non-invasive mechanism for differentiating cancer from normal tissue in real time, which limits our ability to spare healthy tissue and ensure removal of all cancer cells.It is possible that this therapy may provide a benefit to your dog, but there's no guarantee. Possible benefits include:ability to differentiate cancer from normal tissue, enabling us to remove all the tumor tissue and improve patient outcomes immunotherapeutic drug administration (anti-PD-L1) may improve the immune system's response to fight off the cancerPotential RisksAll medical procedures carry risks, and experimental treatments have the potential for increased risks because they have not been used routinely.The investigational drug (anti-PD-L1) and the fluorophore (IRDye-800) have been given before to dogs, separately, without side effects. However, anti-PD-L1 bound to IRDye-800 has never been given to dogs before so there is a risk of infusion reaction as well as unknown other side effects, including potentially fatal reactions.
